Unsupervised domain adaptation (UDA) facilitates cross-domain learning in the absence of target labels by utilizing knowledge from a distinct but labeled source domain. Despite this benefit, UDA does not consistently yield optimal results and has led to reported instances of "negative transfer." This study establishes a straightforward lower bound on the target domain error—a complement to the current theoretical upper bounds—indicating that merely optimizing for low source domain error and minimizing marginal distribution shifts is inadequate, potentially increasing discrepancies in the induced labeling function. This limitation is further evidenced through simple distributional examples where the same UDA strategy can result in success, failure, or an uncertain outcome. Inspired by this insight, we introduce novel data poisoning attacks designed to deceive UDA models into producing high error rates on the target domain when evaluated against standard benchmark datasets where UDA previously excelled. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that even adding just 10% corrupted source domain data drastically reduces target accuracy, occasionally near 0%. These findings underscore UDA's inherent inability to provide consistent cross-domain generalization, aligning with the theoretical lower bounds. Consequently, subjecting UDA to adversarial conditions like poisoning is essential for accurately assessing their robustness against unfavorable data distributions.

We introduce LOCA, a network designed for counting arbitrary semantic object categories from images with either no or only a few labeled examples. While the conventional approach for few-shot counting involves extracting visual appearance features from a sample and matching them with image data to estimate counts—often achieving limited results because feature pooling typically disregards shape data—LOCA improves accuracy by integrating this missed information. Our primary innovation is an object prototype extraction module that iteratively synthesizes instance shape and visual queries with image appearances to derive object prototypes, extending functional to zero-shot contexts as well. Experimenting on the widely-known FC347 (FSC147) benchmark, LOCA outperforms current leading solutions significantly, achieving a modest to moderate RMSE reduction by one third across shot and non-shot-based counting conditions, while achieving leading performance and enhanced adaptability in zero-case.

We have introduced a volumetric communication platform designed specifically to support procedural remote assistance. Within this system, a remote expert provides visual guidance to a local operator by sharing a spatially identical viewpoint; however, the local user interacts with physical objects on-site, whereas the remote expert perceives them as holographic projections in a mixed reality environment. Instruction facilitates verbal cues alongside gestures, while direct spatial notes or annotations appear on both the local object or their corresponding digital avatar. Users at each end utilize mixed reality spectacles for this comprehensive spatial visualization and communication process.

Collective cellular migration, defined by sustained contact and synchronized movement between cells, is pivotal in embryonic development and oncology. Contemporary imaging studies have generated temporal trajectories of individual cells, offering new insights into tumor spheroid expansion. Results from both computational and experimental approaches reveal that central cells within spheroids display subdiffusive glassy behavior, described by a mean square displacement scaling as $\Delta(t) \approx t^{\alpha}$ with $\alpha < 1$, while peripheral cells show superdiffusive kinetics with $\Delta(t) \approx t^{\alpha}$ where $\alpha > 1$. This superdiffusion in outer regions stems largely from strong persistence in correlated directional movement. Strikingly, the extracted $\alpha$ coefficients for core and periphery from simulations closely matched those from experiments without any adjustment parameters. Furthermore, the qualitative distinction in dynamics is characterized using the fourth-order susceptibility, a metric typically applied to metastable states in glass formers. Velocity autocorrelation analyses expose significant spatial heterogeneity, with individual cell behaviors showing no two instances being nearly alike. The hypothesis that the diffusional index $\alpha$ correlates with cellular position offers a clear avenue for experimental verification. Finally, the highly variable dynamics of cells within the spheroid offers a viable explanation for tumor heterogeneity.

This article presents an innovative approach to robot control known as Pose-Based Tactile Servo (PBTS) using soft tactile sensors. PBTS operates by integrating a model for estimating the sensor's position and orientation within a servo control system, specifically targeting local features on objects such as surfaces and edges. Facial Expression Recognition (FER) plays a crucial role in modern human-computer interaction systems; however, current methods frequently struggle with significant performance declines on non-frontal faces. Generating cross fields is typically fundamental to creating block-structured quadrangular meshes; however, singularities within these fields critically determine the mesh's final architecture. This study extends Ginzburg-Landau methods to incorporate a new user-controlled framework for specifying internal singularities. Additionally, a method is presented to approximate the Ginzburg-Landau energy for cross fields defined over this perforated area by solving an associated Neumann linear problem, with the resulting energy approaching the functional limit as the parameter epsilon and the hole radii diminish. To better understand the total sum of the degrees associated with these internal singularities, we provide: (i) an expanded Ginzburg-Landau formulation tailored to piecewise smooth domains for identifying boundary singularity locations and magnitudes, and (ii) a focus on interpreting degrees of freedom while analyzing internal singularities specifically within the context of the Poincaré-Hopf theorem.

The rise of contextualized language models has significantly improved search outcomes, both by fine-tuning traditional weighting schemes like BM25 through re-ranking and by enabling direct passage indexing and retrieval known as dense retrieval. This paper presents a comprehensive side-by-side evaluation, identifying specific scenarios where each method succeeds or fails in comparison to its counterpart as well as a standard BM25 baseline. The findings indicate that although ANCE is superior to ColBERT in terms of processing speed and memory efficiency, multiple representations yield statistically higher performance based on MAP and MRR@10. Furthermore, multi-sentence vectors deliver greater relative improvements over single vectors when tackling queries that challenge BM25 the most, definitional queries, or inquiries demanding complex information synthesis.

Online optimization represents a recognized paradigm dedicated to constructing a sequence of valid choices with the benefit of prior solution information from earlier stages. Over the last few years, precision medicine has experienced substantial progress, particularly in developing algorithms designed to derive patient-specific treatment rules (ITR) that optimize outcomes by mapping treatment covariates. Traditional Direct Learning (D-Learning) offers a one-shot approach to estimating ITRs through the direct modeling of treatment-covariate interactions, yet it fails to account for scenarios where outcome variance is heteroscedastic relative to treatment assignments and covariates. The method proposed here, Stabilized D-Learning (SD-LLearning—or simply S-Learner when used generically), addresses this omission by utilizing the heteroscastic structure in the residuals. It applies residual weighting to integrate flexible models—such as XGBoost and random forests—for variance estimation. Furthermore, an internal cross-validation process identifies the optimal residual model across various candidates. By incorporating these elements, S-Learner improves upon the efficiency of D-Learner both in binary and multi-arm treatment contexts. It serves as a user-friendly augmentation to existing D-Learner variations, such as Angle-based and Robust D-Learner methods. The theoretical optimality of this approach has been scrutinatively examined, while simulation results comparing it directly against standard D-Learner methods demonstrate superior performance regarding empirical loss, error metrics (APE), classification accuracy, as well as real-world application on clinical data.

Text recognition within computer vision is an intensely researched field that, despite significant recent advances toward practical "in-the-wild" applications, remains hampered by a critical deployment issue: existing methods often fail when recognizing novel or infrequent character sequences. To address this "unseen" sequence problem, we introduce a novel, iterative framework where prior predictions enhance the primary model to facilitate subsequent improvements. A pivotal element of our approach is an enhanced cross-modal Variational Autoencoder (VAE) functioning as a feedback loop, optimized using textual error distribution. Specifically trained on error metrics, the module converts predicted character outputs into continuous affine transformation parameters that modulate visual feature representations for the following stage. Evaluation on standard benchmarks reveals that our method matches leading-performances. Crucially, under a disjoint experimental setup where training and testing labels never overlap, our model delivers the superior results to date, demonstrating its ability to generalize effectively to truly unseen words.

To study how magnetic fields influence the development of the interstellar medium, the birth and lifecycle of molecular clouds, and the creation of stars, it is necessary to determine their three-dimensional (3D) structure. Recently, innovative techniques have emerged for detecting distinct components separately and combining this data, alongside models and other sources of information such as galactic field inclinations, to reconstruct 3D magnetic fields. This review evaluates such advancements along with their current applications and prospective future trajectories.

In solid-state physics, crystal energy calculations typically rely on solving Kohn-Sham equations via plane-wave discretization; however, resolving Coulomb singularities often demands large plane-wave cut-offs for accuracy. This paper investigates the plane-wave convergence of eigenvalues associated with periodic linear Hamiltonians featuring Coulomb potentials, using the variational projector-augmented wave (VPAW) approach. Within the VPAW framework, an invertible coordinate transformation is applied to the initial eigenvalue problem specifically within local regions surrounding the singularities ("balls"). Consequently, this process results in a generalized plane-wave eigenvalue problem. It demonstrates that VPAW significantly suppresses the steep cusps in the eigenfunctions at atomic nuclei. While these modified functions introduce discontinuities in their higher-order derivatives at the sphere radii, balancing these two error sources reveals that VPAW yields dramatic improvements in plane-wave convergence for eigenvalues with only a trivial increase in computational effort. Numerical validation tests further support this method as being highly efficient in handling Coulomb singularities.

This study addresses a coordinated vehicle platooning challenge on a road network with specified vehicle routes and time limits, aiming to synchronize departure times for platoon creation and thus optimize total fuel savings. Here, each vehicle's temporal flexibility can be uniformly described so that synchronizing departures corresponds directly to managing time-window overlaps. Leveraging this insight, we develop a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) formulation based on window over-laps, which aligns with previous continuous-time approaches in the continuous case. Applying an adaptive time-discretization step further refines this into a vehicle-to-time-bucket assignment-based MILP. Unlike continuous formulations, the assignment model avoids big-M coefficients; numerical results confirm its superior computational performance. Additionally, as a contribution of its own, we introduce three approximation algorithms with provable competitive ratios for this discrete optimization problem, assuming specific regular conditions—anachief not previously accomplished in this area for loop-free cases. We extend this methodology to general network instances where route graphs may contain loops by integrating a systematic loop-breaking technique. Notably, we discovered that the existence of an exact equivalent assignment formulation for these general instances strongly relates to the structure of underlying lattice groups.

Programming languages offer extensive support for dynamic features, allowing implementations to adjust to varying usage contexts and facilitate code reusability, particularly for data binding, user interface builders, and object-relational mapping. Although beneficial, relying on these features introduces vulnerabilities by compromising the reliability of static analyses essential for tasks like bug discovery and program repair, while also reducing compile-time safety. The reflective code resulting from these features can lack clarity, leading to potential misuse and increased susceptibility to software errors. This research aims to measure specific repercussions of employing dynamic features in Java, concentrating on their contribution to a specific bug category: single statement errors. Drawing from an analysis of 2,024 GitHub projects, researchers identified 136 single statement bugs distributed across ten recognized classes. The data indicates a predominance of errors originating from three frequent pattern types. These findings enable developers and practitioners to assess the comparative dangers of utilizing dynamic approaches versus alternatives such as code generation tools, while also prompting a heightened awareness of which dynamic interfaces are most hazardous during the selection process and aiding in the future design of specialized detection tools

We demonstrate that this technique minimizes both the quantity and periodicity of essential communication exchanges compared to current alternatives while maintaining optimal efficacy, establishing theoretical convergence assurances for quasi-self-concordant objectives, such as those arising in logistic regression.

It is established that impulsive systems featuring nonlinear, time-varying, or switched dynamics are both input-to-state stable (ISS) for bounded inputs and integral input-to-state stable (iISS), provided they admit global weak linearizable stability. A system permits this type of stability if its transition and jump functions are expressible as a (possibly switched or time-varying) linear component augmented by a nonlinear perturbation that satisfies a state-dependent affine bound; importantly, this bound becomes linear when inputs are zero but avoids enforcing global linearity under zero input. These findings broaden and surpass prior results through several improvements: (a) they impose no constraints regarding dwell-time or other limitations on the sequence of impulse instabilities, (b) they apply to systems that are not linear when inputs are zero, (c) they do not require a (common) Lyapunov function, and (d) they relax requirements on the perturbation boundary not being restricted to linear dependence on the input.

Notably, deviations due to the modified Law appear exclusively in the clustering parameter, as the overall structure of the equations remains consistent. To illustrate how corrections alter the clustering timescale, we compare the modified clustering parameter with its original equivalent. Furthermore, we explore the potential for system symmetry breaking by examining trends in specific heat as system temperature increases.

Consequently, this approach establishes that the conditional probability distribution, restricted to the non-absorption scenario, converges exponentially in total variation to an alternating sequence of probability measures. Furthermore, the specific circumstances under which this alternating pattern reduces to a single, unchanging limit (effectively forming quasi-stationary behavior) are defined. Additionally, the formulation provides characterizations and an upper bound for the spectral gap between the semigroup's leading eigenfunctions and subsequent ones. Finally, the work presents estimates for the ergodic properties of the non-absorbed condition process, commonly termed the Q-process, alongside quasi-ergodicity assessments for the primary Markov chain.

Vector space approaches for handling symbolic data, which map symbols into high-dimensional random vectors, are widely known as Vector Symbolic Architecture (VSA) and, alternatively, Hyperdimensional (HD) computing. This study proposes the Vector Function Architecture (VFA) as a generalization wherein continuous inputs are embedded such that their representation similarity, measured by vector inner products, acts as a specific kernel function. Mirroring VSA principles, vector operations on these representations correspond precisely to defined operations within a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. We examine Fractional Power Encoding (FPE), a randomized encoding technique based on raising a base vector to fractional powers. This analysis reveals that the probability distribution governing the sampling of the base vector dictates the form of the resulting FPE kernel, effectively defining a specific set of computable functions—namely, band-limited ones. By aligning VSA's algebra with kernel machine concepts as pioneered by Rahimi and Recht, random feature methods can be enhanced to handle large-scale computations within this VSA-style framework without altering functional outcomes. The proposed architecture demonstrates practical efficacy through successful results in pattern recognition, non-linear regression, and density analysis. Collectively, these findings establish VFA as a robust theoretical and algorithmic tool for managing functional computation within distributed neural networks, offering versatile potential across multiple artificial intelligence domains while inheriting the benefits of random Fourier features.

Bayesian inference serves as a robust method for estimating parameters in geophysical forward models while quantifying their uncertainties. This study examines Badlands, a simulation tool designed to replicate landscape and basin dynamics across diverse spatiotemporal scales. The model requires accurate inference of various geophysical variables, such as estimating both historical sediment deposition stratigraphy and current surface topography. This inference process is fraught with difficulties arising from sparse data availability, high sensitivity to parameter adjustments, and the inherent complexity of the Badlands model itself. To overcome these hurdles, we propose *Bayeslands*, a Bayesians-based methodology that employs Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling. This newly introduced framework successfully merges information from the sophisticated forward Badlands model with observational datasets and prior historical knowledge, offering solutions to the inverse problem. Utilizing both hypothetical and actual terrain datasets, we analyzed the effects of rain volume and lithology on model outputs by utilizing precipitation and erodeability rates as our two inference parameters simultaneously. Model tests demonstrated that this Bayesian method produces credible probability distributions of the parameters concerned; however, we underscore the persistent challenges of sampling non-tradition multivariate posterior distributions resulting from a highly intricate likelihood landscape that frequently exhibits numerous alternative optimal and less-optimal solutions.

Integrating range sensors with color cameras holds significant promise for robotic tasks such as navigation, semantic understanding, object manipulation, and teleoperation. While numerous methods have combined depth and color data for various applications, most encounter challenges including noise in range measurements and resolution mismatches, particularly given that current range sensors offer lower resolution than color cameras. Our work introduces a novel TOF-stereo fusion technique based on an optimized seed-growing approach. This method projects TOF data onto stereoscopic imagery to establish an initial correspondence set or "seeds." These seeds are then propagated utilizing a Bayesian framework that merges visual similarity scores with depth priors derived from low-resolution range data, ultimately producing accurate depth maps at the native resolution of color cameras. Our approach significantly surpasses 2D pure-stereo algorithms and achieves superior results compared to state-of-the-art sensors like the Kinect, while demonstrating potential real-time execution on a standard CPU.

In studies involving magnetic field calculations for cylindrical permanent magnets, it is customary to model them as ideal, azimuthally symmetric solenoids. The results demonstrate excellent concordance between the experimental data and theoretical models. These findings substantiate the efficacy of using ideal solenoid models to forecast the magnetic field distributions emanating from cylindrical permanent magnets.

The task of learning to search involves training autonomous agents to employ search interfaces for retrieving information. Our work generalizes prior efforts by introducing a hybrid environment that integrates discrete query refinement operations with an initial retrieval stage driven by a dual encoder. Evaluations on the BEIR dataset demonstrate that search agents developed through behavioral cloning surpass the baseline system comprising both a hybrid retrieval and a query-specific re-ranked component. Additionally, we found that incorporating heuristic-based Hybrid Retrieval Environments can boost baseline metrics, significantly improving the nDCG leaderboard for learning-to-research systems. Finally, an in-depth qualitative examination provides further insight into the operational strategies of these agents.

A novel spatial active noise control (ANC) technique is introduced, relying on the individual kernel interpolation of both primary and secondary acoustic fields. Unlike methods restricted to fixed geometries, this spatial ANC approach leverages multiple secondary sources and microphones to suppress unwanted primary noise across an uninterrupted area, offering flexible array configurations through kernel-based field interpolation for effective attenuation over target regions. Additionally, by incorporating a directional-weighted kernel function, the system can prioritize known arrival directions of primary sources, addressing limitations found in prior work where such directional weights were applied uniformly to a combined sound field rather than to the individual primary component, thus restricting performance gains. The proposed strategy facilitates the independent reconstruction of primary and secondary fields and integrates them into a normalized least-mean-square algorithm based on this dual interpolation framework. Experimental validation demonstrates that this individual field interpolation method achieves superior noise reduction compared to approaches utilizing kernel interpolation of the aggregate sound field.

Accurate models depend fundamentally on the quality of their training datasets, a connection that remains increasingly elusive within highly overparameterized deep architectures. To better unravel these obscure causal dynamics, influence methods aim to clarify interactions by measuring precisely how individual training samples shift the ultimate model output. While calculating this influence perfectly can be provably difficult under extreme conditions—prompting the creation of approximate estimators—these tools offer valuable insights despite their imperfections this comprehensive review details. We initiate the survey by establishing rigorous definitions for varying and occasionally conflicting interpretations of data influence. Subsequently, a systematic classification organizes current methods of influence evaluation; each is examined with specific attention to theoretical assumptions, computational complexity, practical constraints, advantages, and drawbacks. Furthermore, identifying gaps leads our proposed pathway for enhancing future utility, ensuring greater practical relevance alongside stronger theoretical and experimental validation. An updated collection of relevant references can be found at the provided GitHub repository.

Achieving decarbonized energy systems depends on expanding both renewable generation and grid flexibility. This study compares how six distinct capacity expansion models handle this issue, analyzing the deployment of peak/base-load generation, transmission networks, and electricity storage. To isolate specific technological influences, we establish four simplified and harmonized scenario pairs that limit focus to just one or two particular technologies in each. The results reveal that differing assumptions about technology unavailability almost universally generate significant variations in recommended optimal expansion across use cases. Regarding storage, assuming fixed energy-to-power ratios can wholly reshape optimal expansion, notably altering the mix between short- and long-duration solutions. Constraints on initial and terminal storage capacity similarly influence the seasonal utilization of long-distance assets. Furthermore, dispatch models featuring pre-order commitments deviate substantially from linear optimization; their restricted foresight and reduced flexibility drive higher capacity expenditures. Methodologies relying on simplified net transfer capacity also tend to undervalue required grid infrastructure compared to precise alternating or direct current load-flow methods. Additionally, geographic disparities in optimal storage and transmission expansion appear linked to distinct regional patterns in renewable generation potential and electricity demand. We conclude that these general observations from our stylized framework largely persist in more sophisticated models, even if they become less pronounced.

This paper introduces Multi-Narrative Semantic Overlap (MNSO), an important though largely understudied NLP task that requires creating a Semantic Overlap from several alternative narratives. Experimental outcomes demonstrate that the SEM-F1 metric aligns better with human judgments and shows superior inter-ruer agreement compared to ROUGE.

The resulting output provides not only the eigenvector distribution and observables but also a reliable uncertainty quantification that outperforms conventional regularization techniques. Consequently, this algorithm offers promising applications across diverse domains in both quantum computing.

This work investigates Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) approaches for approximating incompressible Navier-Stokes equations. Specifically, it examines a scenario where the snapshots, generated using a full order of accuracy model (FOM) with one discretization for the nonlinear term, employ a distinct discretization for that term during the reduction via POD. The analysis demonstrates that a new error component emerges in mismatched cases, matching in scale with FOM errors; consequently, the convergence speed of POD remains largely unchanged compared to scenarios utilizing identical discretizations. Additionally, the impact of implementing grad-div stabilization—or its omission—for both FOM and POD schemes is assessed, revealing that the stabilization enables error estimates independent of inverse viscosity terms. These theoretical conclusions are validated through various numerical experiments.

This study presents various numerical approaches to analyzing Riemannian shape for 3D surfaces under the context of invariant, second-order, elastic (Hilbertian-type) Sobolev metrics. Specifically, the work focuses on calculating geodesic distances and paths—both intrinsic—to parametrized objects and those without intrinsic parametrization, modeled explicitly through imported 3D meshes. Leveraging these foundation techniques, we have constructed corresponding tools for statistical shape analysis across sets of surfaces. Key techniques implemented include computing Karcher means, performing tangent Principal Component Analysis (PCA) over populations, and calculating parallel transport along surface curves. The primary methodology utilizes a relaxed variational framework for solving optimal matching (geodesic matching) problems by incorporating fidelity terms associated with varifolds that achieve reparametrization independence. Furthermore, this relaxed structure permits the comparison and analysis of surfaces with disparate sampling densities and mesh configurations of varying complexity. The paper also details how this relaxed variational structure applies to partially observed shape data. The proposed numerical methodology is illustrated through examples involving both artificial and real-world datasets, showcasing its versatility.

Detecting female oocyte transit to the Falcopian tubes remains a pivotal, unsolved problem for clinicians addressing infertility through methods such as natural cycles or in vitro techniques. The thermodynamics of a Kerr-AdS black hole is reexamined within the context of a restricted phase-space framework, which treats the central charge ($C$) of the corresponding dual CFT and its conjugate chemical potential ($\mu$) as thermodynamic variables, deliberately omitting pressure and its conjugate volume. The analysis reveals that Kerr-AdS thermodynamics closely mirrors previously observed behavior of the charged RN-AdS case. Specifically, system states exhibit first-order supercritical phase equilibria between $T-S$ variables when angular momentum is finite. However, in scenarios with zero angular momentum or at fixed rotational speeds, the transition invariably moves a system from an unstable small black-hole state to a stable large one, without passing through equilibrium. Furthermore, the interplay of the pressure and its conjugate variable induces a Hawking-Page phase transition. Because solving the equations for the complex Kerr metric is intricate, exact critical values and Hawking-Page temperatures are derived strictly within the slow-rotation limit; nevertheless, the fundamental thermodynamic properties remain independent of this specific approximator.

This work investigates electron transport within a Kitaev wire connected via its ends to normal metallic leads characterized by distinct temperature gradients and chemical potentials. Such scenarios are typically analyzed through either the nonequilibrium Green's function (NEGF) formalism or the scattering approach. The NEGF methodology describes current and other steady-state characteristics using Green's functions derived from wire parameters interspersed with self-energy corrections due to coupling to leads. Conversely, the scattering approach examines transport via plane wave amplitudes incident on the wire from reservoir boundaries. The authors explicitly demonstrate that despite these distinct formalisms, both yield identical conductance predictions for the Kitaev chain. Furthermore, we reformulate the NEGF conductance expression to establish a precise one-to-one mapping between NEGF terms and specific scattering amplitudes—namely normal and Andreev reflections/transmission—deriving corresponding closed-form expressions for each. Additionally, we determine the wavefunctions of the zero-energy Majorana bound states (MBSs) in the wire-device coupling, confirming they remain confined to the identical parameter regime found in the isolated Kitaev wire. These MBSs facilitate perfect Andreev reflection that drives a quantized conductance peak at zero bias; this peak broadening correlates inversely with the increase of the MBS weight in the reservoirs when varying specific Hamiltonian parameters.

Reusing recorded audio, commonly referred to as sampling, is a fundamental element of Electronic Music Production (EMP) that dates back to the genre's origins and underpins styles such as hip-hop and jungle. Consequently, OOD detection specifically for fine-grained scenarios remains largely unexplored. Addressing this gap, our study introduces large-scale, carefully constructed datasets where state-of-the-art methods struggle, revealing that even training with a variety of diverse outliers fails to fully cover the broad region characteristic of fine-grained OOD samples. We introduce Mixture Outlier Exposure (MixOE), a method that blends in-distribution (ID) data with training outliers to enhance coverage across different granularities of OODs, and optimizes the model so that prediction confidence decreases linearly as inputs shift from ID to OOD. Comprehensive experiments and analysis confirm MixOE's efficacy in developing robust OOD detectors for these environments; the code is accessible at https://github.com/zjysteven/MixOE.

The concept of graph filters offers a powerful framework for developing generative models regarding networked data, as the outcomes resulting from numerous network dynamic examples can essentially be interpreted as the passing of such a filter. Given this perspective, established signal processing techniques, including frequency analysis with equivalent graph-appropriate meanings, fruitfully contribute to data science, uncovering novel understandings for these fields. Below is an interactive walkthrough catering specifically to data produced by low-pass generating graph filters—those models characterized by damping higher graph frequencies while preserving lower ones. It is the widespread utilization of such frameworks within social networks, financial markets, and power systems that informs this selection. We demonstrate strategies for utilizing attributes of low-pass filters to infer graph structure or reveal community organizations, to condense graphs via effective sampling, to restitution lost measurements and purify data against static noise; furthermore, the inherent low-pass characteristic benchmarks the process to spot anomalies.

Generic driven-dissipative quantum systems typically fail to adhere to basic formulations of detailed balance derived from time-symmetry in correlation functions. However, this study demonstrates that such systems can possess a concealed form of time-reversal symmetry, which becomes most apparent within a doubled system framework specifically prepared as an entangled thermofield double state. This latent time-reversal symmetry holds significant practical value, offering a universal strategy for deriving exact solutions to complex steady states; particular instances incorporate established techniques from quantum optics like coherent quantum absorbers and complex-$P$ functions. Furthermore, evidence of this hidden symmetry is observable in individual system experiments, where it can be disrupted by synergistic effects of driving, nonlinearities, and thermal noise in intricate ways. Using model scenarios involving driven qubits and nonlinear cavities, we illustrate these principles, showing that while these systems display hidden time-reversal symmetry, they simultaneously lack traditional detailed balance.

Manually analyzing electrocardiogram (ECG) signals is time-consuming for cardiologists; consequently, machine learning (ML) approaches to automate this task have gained significant attention to automatically detect heart abnormalities by recognizing heartbeat features. However, the lack of interpretability in Deep Learning often limits its use in healthcare. Gaining access to these models allows researchers to understand decision-making processes and the patterns used for specific classification tasks. This thesis constructs and evaluates Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) and Long Short-Term Memory (STM) classifiers, leveraging state-of-the-art architecture while benchmarking them against traditional shallow classifiers, alongside a specific focus on both global and local interpretability methods. To understand variable interactions across the dataset and dissect specific model decisions per sample, the study applies Partial Dependence Plots, Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) values, Permutation Feature Importance, and Gradient-Weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM). The primary emphasis lies on the Grad-CAM method, serving as a local interpretive tool used to investigate differences in model explanations between correctly and incorrectly classified ECG beats. Classifier effectiveness was validated through rigorous validation methods, namely K-Fold cross-validation and a Leave-Greatest-Outs strategy. To determine if observed discrepancies were statistically significant, the research utilized non-parametric statistical tests. Ultimately, the study confirms Grad-CAM to be the most effective interpretive tool for the proposed CNN and LSTM models. A shared conclusion among these high-performance models indicates they primarily rely on the appearance of a healthy QRS complex within the rhythms during the prediction process rather than other signal characteristics.

Current access to quantum hardware enables small-scale execution of quantum machine learning (QML) algorithms. These experiments advance the exploration of quantum computing applications by evaluating the feasibility of prospective methods for the coming era. In this work, we present quantum-based learning of a two-qubit (4x4) unitary matrix utilizing three sequential parameterized quantum circuits totaling twenty-one variational parameters. Additionally, via a variational approach, we extract the unitary's spectral decomposition by determining its eigenbasis, thereby showcasing its utility as an accelerated step within dynamical quantum simulations for state space compression, significantly mitigating circuit depth. Our setup serves as an instance where entanglement amplifies learning efficacy: the reconstruction is performed using only a single pair of correlated, entangled quantum measurements rather than classical large training datasets.

The author explores, evaluates, and contrasts four current and developing runtimes designed for high-performance computing (HPC): Cilk, Charm++, ParalleX, and AM++. This analysis is examined across three dimensions: the programming paradigm, the execution mechanism, and how systems map onto underlying hardware models. The study reviews the programming models and their associated execution environments of these systems, highlighting their declared features alongside goals for performance and developer efficiency. The comparison starts with a qualitative phase focused on programmability, clarifying differences in syntactical expressiveness and semantic structure through shared coding examples common across the platforms. Subsequently, each runtime's execution strategy is scrutinized; this layer connects the programming abstraction to hardware realities. The investigation then assesses four proven implementations representing these paradigms: Intel IPP-based HPX, Cilk, ParalleX, and AM++, specifically noting how recent systems like HPX, Cilk, ParalleX, and AM++ reflect their design principles—using Charm++, Cilk, ParalleX, and AM++ in that order within the context of mature implementations. As future generations of supercomputers expand significantly in scale, parallel programming models must evolve to tackle these emerging obstacles. Rather than designating a superior model among them, the work concludes with a discussion of key takeaways. These reflections demonstrate the value such research holds in shaping and advancing future parallel programming frameworks, ensuring they can adequately meet the challenge of increased scale.

Recent findings indicate that circumbinary discs are often tilted relative to the binary orbit. In such geometrically complex and non-spherical environments, differential precession can trigger warps. While the dynamics of the gas are understood, the behavior of dust in these settings remains largely unknown. This study analytically examines the formation of dust traps within these misaligned discs and demonstrates that "pile-ups"—typically attributed to pressure maxima here—can instead arise from differential precession between the gas and the dust. This disparity in rotational rates suppresses radial drift at two specific locations, resulting in dual dust ring systems whose positioning relies on system-specific parameters, likely affecting particles in the marginally coupled regime (St$\,\gtrsim\,$1) due to significant forces. Our investigation further utilized three-dimensional Smooth Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) simulations across various parameters, including stellar mass ratios, disc thickness, and radial extension, confirming that the results align well with theoretical predictionsUltimately, these dust accumulation sites inhibit drift and support dust growth, thereby enhancing the potential for planet formation.

This letter presents the findings from a spatial energy analysis of the inviscid linear convective instability within a plane incompressible mixing layer. As the onset of absolute instability approaches criticality, the integrated pressure transport term becomes increasingly significant relative to the integrated production term, eventually dominating the energy balance at the exact critical point. This indicates that disturbance amplification thresholds are driven almost exclusively by the pressure transport mechanism, a significant counterintuitive result, rather than the traditional production mechanism. Specifically, the component of the pressure transport term reflecting the work performed by fluctuating pressure forces accounts primarily for the observed shifts in the energy balance. These findings enhance our understanding of the physics behind absolute instability in mixing layers; notably, the redistribution of kinetic energy in the streamwise direction via fluctuating pressure—a "non-local" phenomenon specific to incompressible flows—plays a decisive role.

Collagen fibers stand as the primary structural element of tendons; their characteristic wavy morphology and orderly parallel orientation result in a unique non-linear relationship between stress and strain during elongation. Microstructural models bridge the gap between fiber-level mechanics and whole-tendon properties, enabling the elucidation of mechanisms responsible for specific stress-strain features. Existing research largely focuses on pre-elastic behavior, with scarce attempts to model post-elastic regions without resorting to empirical constructs. This research presents a model based on a strain recruitment framework, utilizing solely microstructural parameters. It separates fibrillar stress into elastic and plastic components, positing that fracture and yield stretches are distributed functions instead of fixed single points. Modifying distribution shapes and their intersection allows for the generation of macroscopic stress-strain curves replicating the entire spectrum of experimental observations, including phenomena unexplained by current models—specifically secondary linear regions post-yielding and stepped degradation after stress peaks. Benchmarking against a prevailing model reveals a substantial drop in average root mean squared error from $4.15 \text{MPa}$ to $1.61 \text{MPa}$, with derived parameters aligning more closely with empirical data. Given that every parameter in the proposed model carries clear physical meaning, it offers the capacity to anticipate how factors like trauma, pathology, and aging alter mechanical performance, contingent on our ability to quantify their impact at the microstructural level.

Research on the influence of demographic variables—including age, gender, and race—on automated face recognition is already mature; however, how digital alterations to these attributes affect such systems remain largely investigated. This study investigates the consequences of facial feature modifications driven by generative adversarial networks (GANs) on face recognition efficacy experiments. Specifically, by manipulating thirteen distinct traits utilizing AttGAN and STGAN within the CelebA dataset, our work evaluates two major verification methodologies, ArcFace and VGGFace, to gauge their robustness. Results reveal that specific changes related to eyewear wear and the synthesis of gender markers can degrade recognition accuracy as high as 73%, suggesting these effects require additional investigation to fully understand and mitigate them.

Automata learning, a method for automatically generating automaton models from query responses, has prompted extensive research into custom adaptations of algorithms tailored for various automata types. The CALF initiative aims to unify these disparate approaches through category theory, thereby facilitating the verification correctness proofs and guiding algorithm development. In this article, we expand CALC by addressing the acquisition of algebraic structures that lack a standard coalgebraic representation. Moreover, we present a rigorous, detailed account of a generalized L* algorithm, a component formerly absent from CALF. By applying this abstract framework to an extensive class of Set functors for the first time, we successfully derive practical tree automata learning algorithms and concurrently formulate novel algorithms designed to learn algebras of quotiented polynomial functors.

A primary challenge in artificial intelligence is constructing embodied systems capable of function within rapidly shifting environmental conditions. These systems require the ability to adapt to evolving task contexts and acquire new information continuously. While conventional deep learning models excel on static evaluation benchmarks, they frequently falter in dynamic environments. In such settings, error cues derived from various contexts often interfere, precipitating a condition called catastrophic forgetting. This study examines biologically inspired architectures as remedies for these issues. We demonstrate that utilizing the biophysics of dendrites and localized inhibitory control allows networks to adaptively constrain and channel information according to specific contexts. Our main contributions entail first, introducing a new neural network framework that integrates active dendrites with sparse representations within standard deep learning practices. Second, we evaluate this architecture on two benchmarks necessitating adaptation based on tasks: Meta-World, an environment for multi-target reinforcement learning with a robotic agent performing diverse manipulation duties, and a continual learning benchmark where prediction objectives evolve during training. Evaluations across both platforms reveal the formation of separate yet overlapping sparse subnetworks, enabling the system to master multiple tasks fluidly while significantly reducing forgetting. This neural approach represents the initial achievement where one architecture competently performs on both multi-task and continual learning frameworks. Overall, this research illustrates how inherent characteristics of biological neurons can be leveraged to design deep learning systems capable of addressing dynamic challenges that typically overwhelm traditional artificial neural networks.

This paper introduces Text-Degradation Invariant Auto Encoder (Text-DIAE), a self-supervised architecture developed to address both document image enhancement and text recognition for handwritten or scene text. We leverage a transformer-based design utilizing three distinct, task-specific pretext objectives optimized via unsupervised pre-training. Ablation studiesvalidate that these specific tasks drive the model's effectiveness. Crucially, our approach overcomes certain limitations found in prior contrastive learning methods and achieves convergence with substantially fewer data samples. Furthermore, our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques within both existing supervised and self-supervised frameworks for text recognition and image enhancement. We anticipate making our code and pretrained models publicly accessible soon at http://Upon_Acceptance.

In electrical circuits containing both capacitive and inductive components, resonances occur based on specific parameter sets and the applied alternating current frequency when measured through admittance. Consequently, this research examines the impedance profiles of unconventional topological electrical circuits (TEs)—specifically 1D and 2D Su-Schrieffer-Heeger (SSH)—to demonstrate the inevitability of size-dependent anomalous impedance resonations in finite $LC$ systems. Utilizing the method of images, we investigate how resonance modes within multi-dimensional lattice arrays undergo modified behavior through the reflection of and interference from boundary currents. Furthermore, we establish analytic formulas for the impedance between opposing corner nodes across various homogeneous or heterogeneous networks and derive integral, as well as dimensionally reduced, expressions for higher-dimensional impencance scenarios. Additionally, we identify the irregular relationship between lattice dimensions and impedance-related resonance while characterizing these specific anomalies.

This guideline is designed to deliver a foundational understanding of adversarial robustness in deep learning, offering a systematic survey of recent methodologies for evaluating how susceptible various DNNs are to adversarial inputs. With an emphasis on state-of-the-art adversarial attack mechanisms and robustness verification techniques, we will further detail promising countermeasures, notably adversarial training, to fortify model resilience. Our goal is to paint a holistic landscape of this growing research field and highlight the critical need for developing robust systems in safety-critical analytical contexts, thereby fostering public confidence in deep learning classification outcomes. Finally, we will outline promising avenues for future inquiry into how adversarial robustness can facilitate accountable and trustworthy data driven applications.

This study addresses the task of generating piano notations in video form given audio recordings and raw handwritten music images, rather than relying on synthetic, preprocessed data as previous approaches did. Our system is designed to handle the disorder often found in raw, unprocessed IMSLP sheet music PDFs, specifically examining its resilience against spam pages, irrelevant sections, and disruptions like jumps and measure continuities. The analysis reveals that accurately processing jumps remains a major bottleneck; notably, a prior proposed "Jump DTW" algorithm lacks the robustness required to detect unknown jump locations. Consequently, we introduce "Hierarchical DTW," a new alignment solution designed to manage jumps without requiring their positions. The algorithm conducts an initial alignment on individual sheet music lines followed by segment-level alignment, which incorporates domain knowledge regarding probable skips. Results from carefully designed experiments conducted on IMPPSF PDF data from online libraries demonstrate that this hierarchical approach significantly outperforms Jump DTW in managing various discontinuous scenarios.

While supernova outcomes and diagnostic data are heavily influenced by the characteristics of their massive stellar parents, most previous studies relied exclusively on one-dimensional, spherically symmetric models. We introduce early simulations of collapse-based three-dimensional progenitors with masses of 12.5 and 15 solar masses, tracked by the hydrodynamical and radiative code Frooxnap from gravitational collapse to bounce. We analyze the explosion dynamics of these complex, 3D models by comparing them to equally massive but still effectively one-dimensionally evolved stars, noting key differences arising from symmetry reduction. We find that accounting for asymmetries in the initial stages increases the likelihood of an explosion. Tensile forces and turbulence within these three dimensions serve as initial patterns for shock wave formation across diverse massive stellar remnants; the identification of gravitational signatures could lead to further investigations regarding noise sources such as pre-supernova shock reverberations detected by gravitational wave instruments.

Collecting these and labelling standards for LiDAR-Camera fusion results indicate that our model has the ability to accurately segmentation and classify apples accurately. Our experimental results show the proposed method performed accurately segmentation on real unstructured orchard data with high-density or noise.

Social media platforms allow users to post on various subjects, where they may receive community feedback such as comments, replies, or retweets on their content. There exists a hypothesis that this volume of feedback impacts which topics users choose to post about; however, validating this proposition proves difficult due to user heterogeneity and external confounders that interfere with isolating the effect. This analysis investigates this idea using a predictive, interpretable framework focused on whether an author revisits the topic of a previous post. We address confounding variables, ranging from intrinsic user topic preferences to unobserved external occurrences like breaking news or social events, by calibrating predictive precision. This strategy allows us to identify specific users susceptible to community influence. Ultimately, our findings reveal that 33% of inactive-but-active Reddit users and 14% of those on Twitter adapt their topic selection based on feedback. The data also indicates that this influence can boost the likelihood of topic repetition by as much as 14%, varying by user and feedback intensity.

Subclassing cancer is vital for comprehending tumor characteristics and determining appropriate treatment; however, current labeling protocols are often clinically contentious and detach subtyping from its educational purpose. Furthermore, genetic expression datasets associated with cancer are characterized as high-dimensional, limited in volume, and complexly interdependent, which significantly challenges existing subtyping models in generating sensible clusters. To address this, we introduce a new unsupervised clustering approach designed to leverage genetic expression data for subtype differentiation. This method dynamically learns categorical relationships linking latent representation profiles to model-derived subtypes. By maximizing problem-agnostic mutual information between input expression profiles and output subtypes, the approach automatically determines the appropriate number of clusters. Empirical results demonstrate that this method refines existing debatable labels, and subsequent medical analysis confirms that these refined subtypes exhibit a high degree of correlation with cancer survival outcomes.

This paper introduces a VirginiaInetRangeingLiAR (VIRAL) SLAM framework, which constitutes a closely coupled, multi-modal localization and mapping system that fuses data from inertial measurement units (IMUs), cameras, various lidars, and Ultra-wideband (UWB) range sensors. Implementing such an all-encompassing sensor fusion requires resolving critical hurdles including data alignment, real-time multi-threading execution, bundle adjustment (BA) optimization, and aligning disparate UWB coordinate frames with onboard sensors to guarantee robust, real-time localization. Consequently, we outline a dual-stage method. Initially, a central odometry thread processes IMU, camera, and lidar data within a local sliding window; the resulting local map generates candidate key frames for inclusion in the global structure while simultaneously applying visual feature-based loop closing constraints to the global factor graph. Once sufficient spatial diversity is achieved within this graph, a BA update computes the relative coordinate transform between UWB anchors and the internal SLAM components, enabling the system to transition smoothly into the second stage, which tightly integrates all available sensors within a shared odometry thread. We validate the system's effectiveness using high-fidelity physical-simulation environments as well as standard public datasets.

Extensive studies within both relativistic and non-relativistic many-body frameworks using various interactions have robustly confirmed the empirical "parabolic law" for the Equation of State (EOS) of asymmetric nuclear matter (ANM). Nevertheless, it remains uncertain whether a fundamental physical basis accounts for the symmetry energy quartic terms remaining significantly smaller than the quadratic terms, especially as ANM transitions toward pure neutron matter. In an examination spanning non-relativistic and relativistic Free Fermi Gas (FFG) systems across arbitrary spatial dimensions $d$—with and without Short-Range Correlations (SRC)—combined with non-linear Relativistic Mean Field (RMF) modeling, we investigated how relativistic kinematics, dimensionality, interactions, and SRCs influence the $\rho$-dependent ratio $\Psi(\rho)$ of qualtic to quadratic symmetry energy. The FFG-derived $\Psi(\rho)$ was determined to be highly sensitive to spatial dimensionality; although negligible already in standard 3D space, it may diminish further in lower-dimensional contexts affecting sub-systems within heavy-ion collisions or neutron stars due to specific symmetries, collective behaviors, or boundary constraints. Theoretically, $\Psi(\rho)$ increases substantially only in the ultra-relativistic limit at densities exceeding those found in neutron stars. In contrast, nuclear interactions exert a profound influence on the density profile of $\Psi(\rho)$—both direct and mediated by SRCs populating high-momentum states—producing deviations from FFG forecasts, whereas relativistic kinematic corrections were found to be minimal regarding this ratio. Beyond altering SRCs within symmetric nuclear matter's kinetic energy and modulating $\Psi(\rho)$ significantly, these insights offer valuable perspectives on the Equation of State for high-density, neutron-rich environments.

Suppressing multi-user interference through precoding is a standard approach for enhancing spectrum efficiency in multiuser MIMO (MU-MIMO) systems, a method whose optimization for high performance and low complexity has dominated the last decade. However, conventional techniques like Zero-Forcing (ZF) and Weighted Minimum Mean Square Error (WMMSE) algorithm fail to provide an optimal balance between computational demands and performance outcomes. To address this, we present a low-complexity precoding framework for MU-MIMO leveraging deep learning, which reformulates MIMO precoding as multiple-input single-output precoding to facilitate closed-form determination of the optimal structure. A tailored deep neural network is employed to map channel states directly to the precoding matrix. Additionally, strategies such as input dimensionality reduction, network pruning, and recovery module compression further boost computational efficiency. Finally, we explore adapting this method for practical MU-MIMO orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) systems, and simulation results confirm that our proposed scheme delivers comparable performance to the WMMSE algorithm at significantly reduced computational costs.

Distinguishing ourselves from studies restricted to specific fields such as the reals or complex numbers, this analysis addresses the generalized scenario, yielding a near-exhaustive understanding. Specifically, over prime fields, the two axioms are interlinked (where additivity entails homogeneity), whereas for non-prime fields of characteristic not equal to two, the conditions stand independently. Finally, regarding non-prime fields of characteristic two, the issue of their relationship remains an open question.

With the growing prominence of 3D point cloud analysis, challenges regarding dataset size limitations and limited network robustness have emerged. To address these issues, we introduce PointCutMix, a straightforward and efficient data enhancement technique for point cloud datasets. The method aligns two point clouds to establish an optimal correspondence, creating new training samples through strategies tailored to varying accuracy or robustness needs. The first strategy randomly selects points to swap, whereas the second leverages the $k$ nearest neighbors of an arbitrarily chosen query point; both yield consistent and substantial performance gains across different model configurations for classification. Integrating saliency maps into this point selection process further amplifies results. Not only does PointCutMix boost model robustness by warding off adversarial point-wise perturbation, but in its capacity as a defense mechanism, it also surpasses current state-of-the-art solutions. The project's source code can be found at https://github.com/cuge1995/PointCutMix.

A generalized low-density parity-check (GLDPC) code modifies the conventional LDPC framework by substituting standard single-parity-check nodes with linear codes that enforce stricter constraints. This paper presents a novel construction technique for GLDPC codes termed the "partially doped GLDPC" (PD-GLDPC). Unlike traditional protograph GLDPC codes, which generalize protograph check nodes by swapping them with complex check nodes, the proposed method extends check nodes to selected variable nodes through insertion, introducing greater flexibility and degrees of freedom. These PD-GLDPC codes facilitate more precise extrinsic information transfer (EXIT chart) analysis and allow for finer doping granularity within the protograph structure compared to standard LDPC implementations. Additionally, we establish a condition for the typical set minimum distance, demonstrating that PD-GLDPC codes meeting this requirement possess linear minimum distance expansion characteristics. We derive optimized threshold prototypes for both regular and irregular ensemble variants of the PD-GLDPC code specifically tailored for the binary erasure channel (BEB). Concrete construction algorithms analogous to regular and irregular forms—enabling higher-rate code generations than standard ones—have been introduced. Performance evaluation via block bit rate analysis indicates that the proposed PD-GLDPC codes deliver robust waterfall behavior and a minimal error floor, surpassing other LDPC codes with identical parameters regarding rate and length.

Domain alignment usually necessitates access to data from the source domain to leverage its distribution characteristics; however, in many practical applications source data is often unavailable for targeted adaptation due to constraints like privacy concerns. A practical yet difficult problem arises, labeled as "source-free unsupervised domain adaptation," where only a pre-trained source model and unlabeled target data can be utilized. To address this, we propose a novel noisy denoising pseudo-labeling technique that enhances model self-adaptation by leveraging the available source model, a task inherently complicated because source models generate inherently noisypseudo-labels due to the severity of domain divergence. To tackle this, we introduced complementary pixel-level and class-level filtering schemes, alongside uncertainty and prototype estimation strategies, which efficiently filter noise and prioritize reliable pseudo-labels to bolster adaptation efficiency. Empirical testing on cross-field funderis imaging for image segmentation indicates our source-model-dependent-free method with untouched source models outclass or equals modern methods reliant on source data.

This study addresses the task of measuring similarity between pairs of news articles. The provided dataset comprises seven distinct objective similarity metrics and contains articles written in various languages. Beyond a baseline using cosine similarity with pre-trained embedding models, a feed-forward neural network was trained to enhance results. Separate feature extraction pipelines were constructed for each of the seven similarity metrics. The outcomes demonstrated a substantial improvement over the baseline when utilizing both these feature pipelines and neural networks.

Recent research suggests that deep neural networks produce receptive fields resembling biological systems; specifically, the neural activity in these artificial networks linearly correlates with mammalian cortical activations in response to identical sensory stimuli. However, the extent to which these systems learn in a manner akin to biological brains remains a mystery. To investigate this, researchers recorded functional UltraSound (fUS) responses from auditory cortices in two ferrets while they heard 320 ten-second audio clips. These recordings were compared with activations derived from Wav2vec 2.0, a self-supervised model trained pretraining on nine hundred hours of speech, but processed using the exact same 320 clips. The evaluation focused on two configurations: the standard "Pretrained" state, and a "Continuous Update" state where model weights underwent back-propagations adjustments sequentially throughout the presentation trial. The findings indicate that activating Wav2vec 2.0 in "Continuous-Update" mode generates neural activity patterns significantly more compatible with biological observations compared to either a static pretraining condition or alternative control models. Consequently, the study suggests that using learning rules that modify neural updates on an ongoing basis mimics the patterned fluctuations seen in cortical activity. Ultimately, these results support the notion that an analogous underlying learning principle links the sound processing capabilities in cortical systems to those in trained artificial models trained with self-supervation mechanisms.

This research analyzes $\Lambda_b^0$ decays into $D\bar{K}^\mp$ final states using 9 fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collision data from an integrated luminosity collected by the LHCb detector. Two specific decay channels are investigated: the direct $\Lambda_b^0 \to D\bar{K}^\mp$ transition with $D\bar{\to } ~0$ or the Cabibb-favored path. While the former is the more probable process, the recombination into the second path occurs via interference. Consequently, we measure both branches' fractional differences and determine their CP symmetry, providing valuable insight into the Cabibb-Kobayashi-Maskawa mechanism angle $\gamma$ with potential constraints on B-photon transitions. We also highlight that the second branch is expected to be significantly smaller. Furthermore, by comparing all known cases where such processes have occurred in other channels before ours can inform expectations about future theoretical models. In summary, this study bridges gaps in understanding how heavy particles behave differently depending on their decay paths.

Q-matroids serve as the q-analog of classical matroids. In this study, we define multiple classes of mappings between q-matroids; these are not invariably linear yet maintain subspace properties and honor the q-matroid structure in specific respects. Diverse map types generate distinct categories for q-matroids, yet we demonstrate that exactly one category supports a coproduct: the one consisting of linear weak maps, wherein an image subspace's rank never exceeds that of the original. Notably, this unique coproduct aligns precisely with the recently defined direct sum of q-matroids.

We propose new smoothing estimators for graph signals, rooted in recently explored Deterrminantal Point Processes (DPPs). Derived by utilizing edge and node selections defined via this DPP, these estimators generate trees and unicycles. Building accurate automatic extraction models for visual-heavy documents, such as invoices, is significantly hampered by the expensive collection of thousands of well- annotated training samples required for robust performance. To address this, we present "Selective Labeling," which streamlines the annotation effort by requiring only binary "yes/no" confirmation for candidate extracts flagged by a model initially trained on sparsely labeled data. Merging this approach with a specialized active learning technique to identify instances where the model exhibits the highest uncertainty, we demonstrate via experiments across diverse domains (encompassing three specific document categories) that Selective Labeling lowers the cost of data labeling by a factor of ten while introducing minimal accuracy degradation.

The study meticulously outlines selection strategies for training algorithms, neural network configurations, and observed parameters, all tailored to accommodate the specific efficacy metrics introduced. Finally, we evaluated the resulting controllers' robustness against sudden rotor power loss and gusty winds before presenting final conclusions regarding the design of practical reinforced learning based controllers.

Improving urban air quality and safeguarding public health represents a paramount concern for authorities, leading to actions such as the creation of Low-Emission Zones (LEZs) to curb major atmospheric pollutants. This paper investigates the automatic prediction of Dialect Affinity Density for African American English (AAE), defining this metric as the proportion of words within an utterance exhibiting features of the non-standard variant. Subsequently, an XGBoost classifier predicts speaker-level dialect density based on these engineered inputs and performs feature selection via analysis during the inference process. The effectiveness of each feature in isolation and in aggregation is thoroughly tested across the corpus. Artificial intelligence-powered computer vision has demonstrated that image and video collections offer significant value for assessing the population size and dynamics of humpback whales (Megalaptera novaegangliae). Social media applications like YouTube generate large volumes of video content from global citizens, providing rich spatiotemporal data regarding whale encounters. This study focuses on automating a binary classification process using deep learning to identify YouTube videos that document genuine humpback whale interactions versus those that do not. By employing an ImageNet-pretrained Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) paired with a Recursive Neural Network (CNNRNN) architecture, the research evaluated video relevancy with notable results. Five-fold cross-validation produced an average classification accuracy of 85.7%, with precision-recall F1 scores reaching 84.7% for negative samples (or irrelevant) videos.

Identifying Many-Body Localization (MBL) often relies on numerical calculations of high-energy eigenstates. Conversely, the present study evaluates techniques designed to detect disorder-induced localization exploiting quantum hardware. For small systems, simulations reveal how magnetization and twist overlap—quantifiable on quantum processors through qubit measurements—transform between the thermal and localization regimes. Additionally, the twist overlap assessed from the post-time-evolution wavefunction, under specific constraints, mirrors that calculated with eigenstates within mid-spectrum energies. Ultimately, measuring this evolved twist overlap across multiple disorder instances proves to be a promising indicator of MBL via quantum computing methodologies.

This contribution outlines a comprehensive framework that integrates vehicle dynamics—emphasizing instabilities and traffic waves—accurate vehicle energy models tailored for highly unsteady driving profiles, and sparse Lagrangian controls suitable for deployment through current automotive technology like adaptive cruise control systems. Served as a fundamental building block, this framework facilitates the creation of control strategies designed to enhance human-in-the-loop traffic flow stability on real-world highways. Throughout, we detail the key advantages of merging vehicle dynamics with energetic modeling into one approach and illustrate, through simulated results, how sparse smoothing control systems influence energy consumption.

This research investigates Shor relaxation in quadratic programming by maintaining a specific feasible set to examine the functional space where exact recovery occurs via the relaxation method. Initially, we outline the circumstances rendering this feasible region invariant regardless of the generators selecting it. Subsequently, we characterize the functional space when the feasible set exhibits symmetry under actions within a subgroup of the $GL_n(\mathbb{R})$ group. Finally, we extend these findings to binary quadratic programs. By providing a specific characterization of objective functions enabling exact Shor relaxation, we utilize these properties to develop an algorithm generating candidate solutions for binary quadratic optimization.

Although requirement engineering (RE) and its reliance on models has expanded within the field, it has rarely found a substantial home in systems engineering, even though modeling techniques are prevalent in systems design at other organizational levels. One explanation is that formal requirements models often struggle to harmonize with current agile development methodologies. Previous research has explored the challenges surrounding both agile practices and the adoption of models but has largely neglected successful implementations of modeling within agile systems engineering environments to bridge this methodological divide. This gap has prompted us to examine practices at Ericsson, a leading telecommunications provider based in Sweden. By observing teams at one of Ericsson's specific branches known for integrating plan-driven activities with agile processes, we investigated these efforts. Our findings reveal that industry participants leverage modeling to visualize inter-requirement connections and monitor product evolution. Yet, recognizing how labor-intensive these efforts have been, they advocate adopting text-based notations. These simplified notations cater more closely to developers and fit seamlessly into existing software workflows without requiring completely new approaches. This choice necessitated a specific trade-off between development workflows and modeling precision, such as the loss of control needed by stakeholders to position and arrange model diagrams precisely.

Calibration remains a critical factor in the user experience surrounding Brain-Computer Interface (BCI) systems. Standard experimental setups frequently mandate extensive training protocols prior to actual usage, which often induce significant cognitive fatigue. To mitigate or eliminate this user-specific calibration burden, researchers are increasingly turning to advanced machine learning strategies, particularly transfer learning, which leverage high-quality pre-training on reference data. Leveraging Riemannian BCI methods, this work introduces a straightforward yet potent scheme for classifying data from multiple distinct contributors with a minimal calibration phase while maintaining robust performance. The paper distinguishes itself by proposing a novel, highly adaptable methodology applicable across diverse paradigms—such as Steadily Stimulated Visually Evoked Potentials (SSVEP), the P300 component for Event-Related Potentials, and motor imagery—which is then validated through an analysis of many heterogeneous datasets. By utilizing the open-source MOABB framework to guarantee the reproducibility of experiments and the rigor of its statistical methodology, the findings demonstrate the universial applicability of the proposed transfer learning technique for enhancing classifier reliability across most BCI task paradigms; however, certain essential characteristics of current transfer learning protocols can still be refined further to drive global improvements of future implementations.

While recent research suggests using learned probabilistic models to guide this process, such methods struggle in domains lacking sufficient training data. Specifically, we learn from partial intermediate solutions generated along the search path. To leverage these insights, we also develop "guided bottom-up search," a new enumeration algorithm that combines efficient backbones established in prior research with on-the-fly probabilistic guidance. We implemented this approach in "Probe," a tool designed for the Syn-GUSeT syntax (SyGuS). Evaluation against literature benchmarks demonstrates that Probe significantly outperforms both standard bottom-up unguided search and existing state-of-art synthesizers trained on prior corpora. Importantly, these improvements do not sacrifice solution quality; Probe maintains high efficiency by generating only marginally more verbose output and avoids redundant case-splitting.

For general spin systems, we demonstrate that if a local Markov chain possesses a contractive coupling, it yields sharp bounds for both mixing time and the modified log-Sobolev constant within a broad spectrum of Markov chains. Building on these general principles, we achieve $O(n\log n)$ mixing time and an $\Omega(1/n)$ modified log-Sobolev constant for Glauber dynamics when sampling random $q$-colorings of an $n$-vertex graph with a graph having constant maximum degree $\Delta$ and $q > (11/6 - \epsilon_0)\Delta$ for a sufficiently small fixed $\epsilon_0 > 0$. Similarly, in the context of the Swendsen-Wang dynamics for a ferromagnetic Ising model on graphs with $n$ vertices and bounded peak, we secure an $\Omega(1)$ modified log-Sobolev constant and an $o(\log n)$ (or logarithmic scale) mixing time provided system parameter configurations satisfy the conditions of the tree uniqueness region, ensuring a mixing time of order $D$.
