The UK's demographic shifts—characterized by rapidly aging cohorts, declining birth rates, and surging demand among the elderly for social care—have created a looming shortage. Currently, about half of all care provision relies on informal support from family or friends. As low fertility and population "graying" reduce the availability of potential caregivers, policy-makers anticipate needing significant future public spending on formal care services. This paper introduces an agent-based simulation of UK care provision where individuals independently decide whether to offer informal care or purchase private help, basing these choices on their health, job security, financial状况, family relationship, and location. Despite utilizing scant empirical data, the model successfully replicates real-world care needs and availability trends. We contend that this approach more accurately reflects the nuances of social care than existing methods by integrating socioeconomic details and mapping care distribution through kinship networks.

To successfully complete real-world duties such as disaster relief, mobile ground vehicles must possess the ability to traverse unpredictable and unplanned landscapes while navigating obstacles. In unstructured environments like forests, discrepancies between actual robot actions and planned behaviors often arise due to dynamic shifts in terrain conditions or changes within the robot itself. Consequently, achieving robust adaptability to maintain consistent performance is vital for traversability. To tackle this challenge, we present a new method involving terrain-aware, self-reflective adaptation that allows robots to generate consistent commands for navigating complex off-road areas, facilitating precise action execution by combining self-analysis with adaptation. Extensive tests conducted with real-world variants of the robot through diverse unstructured terrains demonstrate that this approach enables reliable navigation, outperforming prior techniques.

Driven by surging demand for streaming and music recommendation services alongside advances in audio retrieval frameworks, the task of Music Genre Classification (MGC) has gained significant attention. Although convolutional approaches struggle with efficient encoding and isolation of temporal characteristics, this paper examines broadcast-based neural architectures to enhance localization and generalizability while maintaining a compact size (~180k parameters). We analyze twelve variants across diverse dimensions—including block structure, pooling and normalization strategies, activation functions, LSTM integration, and inception designs—to evaluate specific performance factors. Experimental evaluations across standard datasets (GTZAN, Extended Ballroom, HOMBURG, and FMA) demonstrate our models achieve state-of-the-art accuracy. Ultimately, this study offers valuable insights capable of facilitating compact, broadly applicable broadcast networks for audio and music classification applications.

G gating methods have historically enabled the creation of isolated attosecond pulses (IAPs) by restricting higher-order harmonic generation (HHH) to a single cycle of the driving laser. However, utilizing only one cycle restricts energy gain, making IAP enhancement via long driving pulses challenging in such regimes. This letter introduces a novel approach called pumping ionizing gating (PIG), designed for IAP generation. Rather than using standard ionizing gating, a PIG scheme employs a prolonged pump pulse that dynamically reflects off a rapidly widening plasma grating (FEPG), thereby continuously injecting energy into the ionizing (driving) pulse where they overlap. This interaction zone facilitates frequency upconversion, creating a transient channel that transfers energy from the long-pump pulse to IAPs. Our three-dimensional particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations demonstrate the feasibility of this method across wide-ranging plasma conditions, specifically densities from 0.02n_c to 0.5n_c and modulation depths between 10% and 60%. These simulations confirm the generation of a 330 attosecond laser pulse driven by a 1.6-ps, 1-μm pump, achieving a peak intensity 33 times higher than the original pump and a conversion efficiency of approximately 0.1%.

Defects are prevalent in all ordered media, exhibiting certain universal traits that stem from topological origins rather than the specific physical details of their underlying environments. Despite this robustness, these topological properties often manifest as `unphysical' singularities characterized by energy density profiles that are non-integrable within traditional coarse-grained macroscales lacking in local details of "microphysics."  

To address this limitation, this work presents a systematic method for enriching coarse-gained theories with sufficient microscopic information to achieve thermodynamic consistence and well-posed models capable of simulating defect dynamics and mutual interactions across large systems. Beyond theoretical models, we devise complementary numerical approaches that can simulate energetically driven defect dynamics throughout materials ranging from disordered to soft and crystalline. These approaches extend to order parameters with "head-to-tail" symmetry, like director fields in nematic liquid crystals; they also apply at translation symmetry is broken to amorphous and crystallized materials, liquid crystals. We demonstrate this approach on actual numerical cases.

We detail a computation involving next-to-next-to-leading order (NNLO) QCD corrections for LHC Higgs boson–W boson association production, specifically targeting Higgs decays into $b\bar{b}$. Distinguishing this from prior massless NNLO investigations of the identical process, we account explicitly for massive $b$ quarks. Treating $b$ quarks as massive simplifies the procedure by rendering flavor-specific jet clustering algorithms superfluous; instead, one can utilize standard jet definitions to isolate $b$-tagged jets. We examine the discrepancies in fiducially cross-section predictions derived via NNLO calculations for scenarios involving both massless and massive $b$ quarks and compare these against parton shower outputs. Our results indicate $\sim 5\%$ deviations between calculations assuming $b qarks$ are massive versus massless at this specific level. However, significantly more substantial divergences appear when examining selected differential observables and those comparing these fixed-order results against parton-shower approximations.

Muon identification performance at LHCb is characterized using data from \( J/\psi \to \mu\mu \), \( \Lambda \to p\pi \), and \( D^\* \to \pi D^{0}(K\pi) \) decays. The core mechanism relies on hit patterns detected in muon chambers. A momentum-dependent binary cut initially suppresses the hadronic contamination level to 1% while maintaining an efficiency of 95–98%. Subsequently, a discriminator is constructed to evaluate the likelihood ratios between muon and non-muon classes. Imposing this condition raises the overall efficiency to 93% while further reducing the hadronic non-identification probability to below 0.6%.

The underwater acoustic environment represents one of the most difficult obstacles in communication systems because of periodic variations caused by tides and daily climate changes. These fluctuations cause the noise—and consequently the quality of the communication channel—to shift cyclically over the long term, which can result in packet routing failures. To mitigate this, researchers have developed channel-aware routing protocols that employ acoustic channel estimation. However, the estimation algorithms currently used are predominantly linear and often fail to account for the periodic nature of the signal. To resolve these issues, our study integrates a model-free approach for SNR prediction using nearest neighbor regression. By addressing the high intricacy and periodical variations found in received Signal-to-Noise Raties, our improved method offers superior predictive precision for complex nonlinear acoustic patterns. To enhance both computational efficiency and storage usage, the algorithm utilizes optimization techniques such as space reduction, statistical storage compression and quick search. Our validation against linear approaches, leveraging sea tests and packet-level datasets, provides clear improvements, with at most threefold increases in prediction accuracy across simulations and operational conditions. Building on the improved channel estimation mechanism, the authors propose the Depth-Based Channel-Aware Routing (DBCAR) protocol to ensure communication links. By integrating channel-aware reliable data exchange and focusing on efficient depth greedy routing, the testing on large-scale datasets shows optimal performance, reducing energy use and packet delay while significantly improving transmission accuracy for users with high packet requirements and bandwidth.

The model outshines inertial models for complex signal traces providing essential data for modern digital timing simulation tool platforms, revealing previously undiected flawed paths, offering an invaluable platform to upgrade current state-of-art simulation methodologies\.

Quantum electrodynamics theory proposes that the vacuum behaves like a polarizable medium, thereby generating effective nonlinear interactions between light fields and enabling phenomena such as light-by-light scattering. A key finding is that collisions between two maximally focused lasers do not yield the strongest observable signal; rather, broadening the focal region typically results in a superior separation of the signal from the background in the far field.

Data-centric AI represents an emerging field within the artificial intelligence landscape. Yet, numerous enterprises have already developed and sustained various "data-centric" solutions designed to generate high-quality data, spanning traditional business processing tasks to production machine learning systems like recommendation algorithms. The domains of data and machine learning engineering have evolved recently to administer these extensive application ecosystems. Through our practical experience deploying these data and machine learning platforms for thousands of applications across diverse organizations, the present paper explores key lessons drawn from these disciplines that hold significant relevance and applicability to advancing data-centric AI methodologies.

Handling advanced real-time social signaling within robotics—particularly in dynamic, multi-user environments—remains a persistent obstacle in Human-Robot Interaction (HRI), especially without a unified model for human representation to enable module interoperability. This paper proposes a set of conventions and ROS-based interfaces aimed at ensuring both interoperability and the reuse of essential HRI tools, ranging from motion capture and face identification to language analysis. Designed for versatility, these tools support diverse applications, including crowd simulation, group-level social modeling, and precise kinematic analysis. We provide a ready-downloadable reference implementation of these interfaces so the community may readily evaluate and test their capabilities.

Algorithms for data assimilation estimate the most probable state of a dynamical system by synthesizing prior models with observational data. Among these, variational approaches, including the weak-constraint 4D variational formulation addressed here, can be characterized fundamentally as minimization tasks. The primary obstacle in these formulations is resolving extensive systems of linear equations required during the nonlinear inner linear step of the solver; these systems may either be symmetric positive-definite (SPD) or saddle point structures. Typically, Krylov subspace methods such as CG or GMRES have solved such systems, but preconditioning is essential to guarantee rapid reduction in the number of required iterations. This study presents novel, efficient preconditioning operators defined through the resolution of particular Stein matrix equations. Beyond delivering superior computational speed and performance, this framework facilitates the derivation of rigorous eigenvalue distribution bounds for the preconditioned system in specific scenarios. Numerical experiments across a wide range of setups confirm the efficacy of this approach, demonstrating its advantage over leading existing techniques.

This study utilizes the local-$\delta{f}$ gyrokinetic code GS2, successfully validated via the GKV benchmark, to investigate flux-surface shaping impacts on the two JT-60SA-related, low-$\beta$ and high-$\beta$ equilibria, each featuring strong shaping effects. Our analysis reveals an unexpected destabilization of electrostatic turbulence caused by enhanced elongation specifically within plasmas characterized by strongly peaked pressure distributions. These findings are attributed to a competition arising between finite-Larmor-radius (FLR) stabilization and the local magnetic shear. Electromagnetic investigations further suggest that heightened shape improves kinetic ballooning stability compared to the ion-temperature-gradient instability by intensifying susceptibility to FLR stabilization. However, it remains true that at elevated $\beta$ levels, increased elongation compromises the magnetic shear stabilization typically associated with reaching the higher stability plateau observed for ballooning modes.

Our findings address both charm and bottom quark masses, with specific inclusion of finite charm-mass effects for the bottom quark case, alongside a determination of four-loop results in the large-$\beta_0$ limit. Achieving deep carbon reductions in the energy sector will demand significant integration of stochastic renewable energy sources and extensive coordination of grid assets, presenting a demanding new challenge for operators who must safeguard grid stability and security amidst this transition. Given machine learning (ML)'s capability to process intricate datasets and generate predictions rapidly, it serves as an optimal tool to navigate these shifts as power systems evolve over the next several decades. We show how sequentially linking specific modulesthat address each of these obstacles enhances the overall efficacy of the machine learning pipeline. Specifically, our methodology connects various pipeline components via a feedback mechanism, thereby establishing an iterative "closing of the loop" between training, assessment, and retraining. By applying this integrated framework with its interactive modules to calculate the N-1 small-signal stability margin for a detailed model of a proposed North Sea Wind Power Hub, the effectiveness of both its components and the feedback structure has been demonstrated.

Certain "quasi-symmetries"—approximate symmetry operations that suffice to affect physical behaviors despite appearing in a lower-order approximation of an effective model and first coined by Guo et al.—form the subject of the present research. In our primary approach, the spin-independent linear momentum (\(k\)) term is designated as the zero-order Hamiltonian, exhibiting four-fold degenerate energy bands protected by an \(SU(2)\times\)SU(2) quasi-symmetry. By treating the spin-orbit coupling (SOC) and the full quadratic-\(k\) components as perturbations (including \(k\)-independent SOC and \(k^2\) terms), the analysis indicates that the first-order correction stabilizes the Hamiltonian via self-commution, resembling a stabilization code and yielding a \(U(1)\) quasi-symmetry that safeguards nodal planes. In our second method, zero-order Hamiltonian construction includes both the free-spin linear-\(k\) term and the momentum-independent SOC term, displaying \(SU(2)\) quasi-symmetry that can diminish to \(U(1)\) based on the configuration of quadratic terms. Accordingly, the initial four-fold band degeneracy associated with the larger \(SU(2)\) group is reduced by quadratic perturbations into protected two-fold degent nodal planes secured by \(U(1)\). Crucially, incorporating perturbations to higher orders disrupts the protecting \(U(1)\) quasi-symmetries for both methods, potentially opening minute energy gaps (of order 1 meV) across what would otherwise remain nodal. These near-degenerate states under quasi-symmetrity shielding are essential for interpreting the most recent quantum tunneling oscillations observed in CoSi.

This letter extends the concept of Krylov complexity, a novel measure of operator complexity known for universal behaviors and serving as a broad benchmark to upper-bound other measures. While previous studies focused on closed systems driven by Hamiltonians, we investigate open quantum systems coupled Markovially to a bath, governed by Lindbladian dynamics. Our analysis demonstrates that within the Hilbert-Krylov basis for such open systems, complexity behavior corresponds to a tight-binding scenario involving a half-chain characterized by non-hermitian terms. Key properties of this framework reveal that non-hermitian coupling strengths grow linearly proportional to an increasing index $n$ in the basis. This non-hermitian structure supports localized eigen-edge modes which define the asymptotic evolution of complexity. Consequently, dissipative interactions suppress the growth of Krylov complexity, causing it to reach a saturated finite limit at long times—significantly lower than the complexity observed in closed systems sharing the same effective Hamiltonian. Numerical simulations on diverse models validate these theoretical findings, particularly the Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model and interacting fermionic frameworks. Ultimately, our results offer new perspectives for examining complexity, chaos, and holographic correspondence within the domain of open quantum systems.

We investigate a system characterized by intrinsic inhomogeneity in interaction strengths or bond disorder. By examining this polar SPP model throughout its order-disorder transition at various degrees of disorder, a notable shift in the nature of this phase transition from discontinuous to continuous becomes evident upon tuning disorder intensity. Furthermore, bond disorder facilitates order enhancement near the critical point by promoting the emergence of a homogeneous flocking state despite substantial levels of disorder. Consequently, intra-system information propagation accelerates and global system information entropy increases. Our work provides novel theoretical insights into how internal inhomogeneity shapes the dynamics of self-propelled particles.

In Phys. Rev. B 102, 144420 (2020), Cabrera-Baez et al. examined the impact of substituting Cd for Zn in the ferromagnetically ordered GdFe$_2$Zn$_{20}$ compound. This indicates that, despite the increase in TC resulting from Cd incorporation, both the low-temperature effective and saturated moments remain stable.

Detecting human-object interactions (HOI) is a crucial advancement for comprehensive machine-driven visual comprehension. While static images suffice for non-temporal HOIs (e.g., a person sitting), it is improbable even for humans to infer time-bound interactions (e.g., a person opening a door) from a single frame given that neighboring frames are essential. Currently, standard methods relying on static images attempt to predic these dynamic events, essentially operating via "guessing" and lacking temporal context, which results in sub-optimal performance. To address this, we detect HOIs in videos by integrating explicit temporal data. First, we observe that a naive temporal-aware version of a standard action detection baseline fails due to feature inconsistency issues. Consequently, we propose Simple yet effective architecture, Spatial-Temporal HOI Detection (ST-HOI), employing temporal clues such as humans and object trajectories, well-localized visual features, and pose information within temporal masking functions. Furthermore, we established a new benchmark dataset called VidHOI to support this approach, where ST-HOI serves as our proposed baseline method for detection tasks on this benchmark dataset.

This paper interprets the elevated braking index of the pulsar PSR J1640−4631 by integrating magneto-dipole radiation with dipole magnetic field decay theories. We define a mean rotational-energy conversion coefficient, $\overline{\zeta}$, representing the total ratio of radiated high-energy photons to rotational kinetic loss over the pulsar's lifetime. Combining high-energy and timing data with a robust nuclear equation of state, we determine an initial spin period of roughly 17–44 ms, which translates into a corresponding moment of inertia between $(0.8$ and $2.1) \times 10^{45} \text{ g cm}^{2}$. Further, assuming a protracted exponential decay in the dipole magnetic field allows us to derive an effective magnetic decay e-folding time ($\tau_D$) of approx. $1.07(2) \times 10^{5}$ years, the true spin-down age between $(2900$ and $3100)$ yrs, and a pole surface field strength at zero time, $B_{\rm p}(0)$, ranging from $(1.84$ to $4.20) \times 10^{13}$ G. We attribute the observed high braking index of $3.15(3)$ to this gradual magnetic decay occurring at a moderate rate, with $\text{d}B_{\rm p}/\text{d}t\approx -(1.66\text{ to }3.85)\times 10^{8}$ Gs yrs${}^{-1}$. Finally, we suggest that this framework accommodates both pulsars with brking indices above and below three, with potential refinements forthcoming from upcoming timing, polarization, and multi-energy analyses of the target.

The semistochastic heat-bath configuration interaction (SHCI) approach combines selected configuration interaction and perturbation theory, delivering near-full configuration interaction (FCI) accuracy systems featuring single or multi-reference traits. However, reaching accurate energies at the complete basis set (CBS) limit is impeded by the sluggish convergence of the FCI energy as the system size expands. We demonstrate that applying a basis-set correction strategy, derived from range-separated density-functional theory, substantially accelerates basis-set convergence within SHCI. Specifically, we explore two variants utilizing different functionals across the range of SHCI calculations, performing these methods on transition metal atoms and monoxides to secure dissociation and individual atom/ionization energies with chemical accuracy.

We investigate priority matching problems constrained by limited farsightedness and demonstrate that when farsightedness reaches an adequate level, outcomes from the Top Trading Cycles (TTC) algorithm attain stability. Specifically, the TTC matching alone forms a horizon-$k$ vNM stable set if agents' farsightedness exceeds three times the size of the largest cycle generated by TTC. In contrast, matchings resulting from the Deferred Acceptance (DA) algorithm may fail to be members of any horizon-$k$ vNM stable set for sufficiently large values of $k$.

This study addresses Bayesian inference in large-scale inverse problems, focusing on the computational burdens imposed by repeatedly running costly forward simulations. Conventional Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) techniques are often unsuitable due to their high sample demands, frequently exceeding thousands of model executions. Additionally, since forward solvers are frequently black-box tools or lack feasible differentiation capabilities, derivative-free solutions are essential. We introduce a framework grounded in Kalman methodology designed to perform such inference efficiently. At its core, this approach approximates a mean-field dynamical embedding of the inverse problem, using the steady state of its filtering distribution's law to represent the desired Bayesian posterior for theoretical linear cases. Proofs of exponential convergence to this steady state are provided, suggesting that for nearly Gaussian nonlinear systems, sequentially updating the law of the filtering distribution forms the basis of rapid iteration. Ensemble methods are employed to approximate this distribution, complemented by strategies like low-rank approximation and a bi-fidelity scheme to reduce memory and compute requirements. Numerical demonstrations validate the method across linear/non-linear test cases and two extensive applications: inferring permeability parameters in subsurface flow and estimating subgrid-scale parameters in a global climate model from time-averaged data.

With deep learning progression, the demand for models synthesizing multi-modal data to tackle complex real-world problems is intensifying. While large multi-modal datasets have recently spurred researchers to develop various fusion techniques, few studies have quantified each modality's specific contribution within these models. This paper introduces SHapley Value-based PErceptual (SHAPE) scores, which quantify both the individual marginal impact of specific modalities and their level of cooperative synergy. Leveraging these metrics, we conducted a systematic assessment of diverse fusion strategies across various datasets and tasks. Our findings reveal two distinct patterns in fusion dynamics: for tasks characterized by complementary but not exclusive modality needs, dominant models often rely on a single primary modality, overlooking potential cross-modal synergy. Conversely, when modalities are strictly indispensable for task success, learning models demonstrate effective exploitation of inter-modal cooperation, suggesting that optimal results are achieved by integrating modalities at earlier processing stages. Ultimately, we anticipate that SHAPE scores will enhance the interpretability of current model behaviors regarding modality usage and motivate the development of more advanced multi-modal integration techniques.

Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) and closely related techniques like Principal Component Analysis (PCA) are extensively used in fields requiring linear matrix factorizations, particularly for clustering and dimensionality reduction. Deep learning architectures are extensively deployed for diverse daily tasks; however, in critical fields such as healthcare or national defense, these systems must be inherently safe and reliable. These models are trained on real or synthesized data combinations to optimize predictability, yet obtaining sufficient, representative data for every conceivable real-world scenario is cost-prohibitive, often restricted by confidentiality, or simply impossible as real conditions continuously evolve into intractable situations. Consequently, a viable strategy involves deploying models that abstain from prediction and signal uncertainty whenever their confidence is insufficient. A key hurdle here is that conventional models typically fail precisely in detecting unreliable, out-of-distribution samples.

To address this, we introduce **TrustGAN**: a generative adversarial network (GANN) framework designed to bolster system caution without compromising performance. TrustGAN is a post-hoc deep learning pipeline that recalibrates an estimated model's confidence for target architectures without altering their predictive capability or requiring internal model modification. This non-invasive nature allows for straightforward deployment within MLOps environments, as it applies universally to any model output providing paired predictions and confidence metrics.

Based on theoretical analysis of the recently developed frequency-to-power converter, we examine a device comprising a hybrid single-electron box with superconducting leads, detected by a thermometer-integrated normal metal bolometer for heat flow measurements aimed at establishing metrology. Primary uncertainties in power readings largely stem from imprecisions in injecting electrons at exact energy levels corresponding to the superconducting gap. To quantify this, we compute the dominant systematic errors arising from excess average energy injected by electrons along with their cumulants and sub-gap current leakage. Using analytic and numerical models, we prove that systematic detection errors can be substantially smaller than injection inaccuracies; moreover, by appropriately tuning system parameters, these errors remain under 1% even with minor adjustments at sufficiently low temperatures. Thus, a configurable optimized system is suggested for precise metrological applications.

Through comprehensive numerical simulations, we examine the flow dynamics of a model binary mixture designed to undergo glass formation, featuring particles with significantly disparate sizes. We focus on studying the rheological response to applied shear specifically in regimes where particles belonging to the larger category are spatially dominant. We show that the increasing density leads to emergent macroscopic rigidity at the specific stage where large particles become glassy and cease moving significantly, while the minor fraction remains highly mobile. We analyze how shear-induced characteristics coexist with quiescent equilibrium relaxation mechanisms across the two particle populations to elucidate these rheological observations from a microscopic standpoint. Additionally, we tune system composition and demonstrate that gradually increasing the inclusion of smaller particles reduces the overall mixture's viscosity.

Beyond simulation insights, the proposed system has been deployed and verified in real-world office settings featuring one to three physical sonar sensors and executing real-time, two-dimensional navigation. By validating various sensor configurations through both simulated and physical experiments, the study demonstrates that this modular integration of controller logic and sensor data processing enables stable, safe navigating of spaces populated with moving objects.

We present both theoretical and experimental investigations into the axisymmetric impact of a rigid sphere impacting an elastic membrane. Utilizing an iterative numerical approach for the associated free-boundary problem, we determine the evolving contact zone where collision forces are applied. Consequently, the proposed simulation accurately forecasts sphere trajectories, membrane deflections, and in-contact pressure distributions, findings which we corroborate using direct experimental data. Furthermore, the work highlights emergent phenomena affecting the coefficient of restitution at low velocities, the occurrence of multi-point contact during individual rebounds, and mechanisms enabling elastic recovery in subsequent jumps. These mechaninsistic insights regarding this model contact problem aim to enhance the formulation and application of predictive frameworks for various engineering contact scenarios.

Directly measuring wall shear stress within turbulent boundary layers (TBL) is difficult; consequently, researchers typically infer these stress conditions indirectly from mean velocity profiles. Leading methods often rely on fitting a fully developed log-law for the inner regions or employing a trial-and-error composite velocity profile across the entire TBL. Both techniques depend heavily on high-quality measurements from the inner layers and frequently struggle or become unfeasible when accounting for surface roughness or pressure gradients, often requiring substantial adjustments. To address this limitation for zero pressure-gradient flows, a new approach is proposed that calculates wall shear stress directly from mean profiles, eliminating the need for measurements very close to the wall. Leveraging a stress formulation previously introduced by Kumar and Mahesh, this method uses just one set of values from the outer region—mean streamwise velocity and shear stress (typically between 20 and 50 % of boundary layer thickness), combined with known boundary layer thickness and shape factors. Unlike existing treatments, this approach remains robust with wall roughness and accurately predicts friction velocity to better than 3 percent for smooth surfaces, rough surfaces, and various Reynolds numbers. To extend these findings, the original Kumar and Mahesh theory is refined into new stress and wall-normal velocity models suitable for zero-pressure-pressure gradients, enabling the derivation of a universal formula to extract wall shear stresses from profile data under varying pressure gradients, demonstrating overall high robustness and accuracy across diverse scenarios.

This study focuses on identifying the optimal stopping time for wood panel glue curing within an automatic manufacturing setting. Employing near-infrared spectroscopy for process monitoring facilitates significant reductions in energy consumption and duration. The approach involves analyzing a collected dataset containing a temporal sequence of near-infrared curves drawn from 72 individual spectra, with the goal of pinpointing this optimal stopping moment. An estimation procedure is introduced to calculate the ideal termination timing for wood panel compression alongside quantifiable uncertainty regarding that estimate. The methodology begins by partitioning the full dataset into distinct training and testing subsets, followed by iteratively computing integrated squared forecast errors based on the testing data. Subsequently, a single-point-of-rupture detection method is utilized on the univariate series of these/errors to identify an approximate optimal stopping time for original data. Additionally, a suite of finite-series simulation simulations assesses the statistical performance of the proposed technique.

We investigate a quantum system initialized in its ground state and driven by a finite-time electromagnetic pulse with carrier frequency $\omega_0$ and an slowly modulating envelope. Solving the time-dependent Schr\"odinger equation for high $\omega_0$, we establish that at leading order in $\omega_0^{-1}$, the system's linear response cancels out precisely when the pulse extinguishes. Despite this cancellation, physical observables remain expressible via a sum of the linear density response and higher-order nonlinear functions of the electric field. Models of jellium slabs and spheres demonstrate that this configuration exhibits exceptional surface sensitivity, yielding a more complex excitation spectrum than standard linear response methods allow. Consequently, we introduce a new spectral methodology tentatively termed Nonlinear High-Frequency Pulsed Spectroscopy (NLHFPS). By uniting high surface specificity, freedom from typical dipole selection rules, and robust interpretability through linear response time-dependent density functional theory, NLHFPS emerges as a promising advanced characterisation technique for fields within nanoscience and nanotechnology.

Tagged magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a prevalent method for quantifying tissue deformation in mobile organs. However, its limited anatomical resolution often requires acquiring an additional, higher-res cine MRI set during sessions for tissue segmentation, resulting in added time and expense. The proposed solution is a dual-cycle constrained bijective VAE-GAN designed to synthesize cine MRI images from tagged ones. This method relies on a variational autoencoder backbone incorporating cycle-reconstruction constraints in the adversarial process, enabling accurate and realistic reconstruction. The framework demonstrated superior performance compared to competitors using independent training, validation, and test sets consisting of 1,768; 416; and 1,450 paired slices from twenty healthy subjects. Consequently, our approach has potential to cut acquisition time and costs without compromising the established workflow for future kinematic analyses.

Trace applies recurrence to segment-wise latent states separated by arbitrary text chunks, utilizing residual parameterization to shape the posterior distribution. We observe that this model enhances the correlation between preceding latent states and each segment, deriving a non-zero lower bound for the KL divergence, which serves as a formal assurance for diverse generation. Empirical evaluation across two zero-shot and one conditional task demonstrates that TRACE substantially improves variety without compromising generation fidelity.

Emotional Voice Conversion (EVC) is designed to transform the affect of a spoken utterance between distinct emotional categories while maintaining both linguistic content and speaker voice quality. Although existing research primarily targets transitions between discrete, specific emotion types, synthesizing blended emotional effects can offer superior imitation of human emotional nuances, thereby enhancing natural human-computer communication capabilities. Pioneering a novel approach in this study, the authors define the challenge of mixed emotion EVC. Emotional styles are treated as a set of learned, ranking-based Support Vector Machine (SVM) attributes, where each measure assesses the intensity relevance of recordings across different emotions. These attributes are subsequently integrated into a sequence-to-sequence framework aimed at emotion variation analysis. During the training phase alongside sequence modeling, the framework both characterizes specific speech styles and quantifies their correlation with various target emotional profiles; conversely, runtime generation of composite emotions allows manual adjustment of these defined attributes. The researchers perform both objective and subjective evaluations to validate these methods and have further developed a Mood Triangle framework as a test application for demonstrating these transitions. Source codes and audio samples have been made available to the public.

Valve-related cardiopathies present a significant challenge in developing regions like Southern Africa, accounting for over 30% of cardiovascular mortality. Enhancing the clinician-specified treatment protocols requires accurate modeling of regurgitative and restrictive defects at the valve level. This research introduces a multi-compliant, lumped-parameter framework for the circulatory system, incorporating an advanced valve simulation method that factors in geometric configurations, regime-specific resistance variations, and cusp dynamics. Utilizing representative human physiological data, the developed framework examines diverse severities of aortic stenosis to evaluate these defects. The new model’s predictions are juxtaposed with those from existing published methods and validated against literature-standard local and systemic indicators, such as ventricular ejection pressures, peak and average trans-valvular pressure gradients, and narrowing velocity measurements. Comparative outcomes reveal that older valve simulation strategies underestimate pressure drops by 47% for peak severity and 30% for mean severity. Conversely, while this new model still underestimates peak pressure drops by 24%, it provides a more accurate average drop by an upward deviation of just 7% when compared against the aforementioned literature parameters.

Training contemporary large language models (LLMs) relies heavily on substantial batch sizes to optimize both throughput and precision, often requiring the handling of diverse sequence lengths on high-performance hardware through padded tokens. This approach ensures sequence uniformity within a batch but incurs significant waste. Our findings reveal that standard natural language processing (NLP) corpora may include up to 50% padding across all tokens—an extreme scenario seen as early as 89% in specific datasets. While existing solutions attempt to mitigate inefficiencies arising from self-attention leaks, reduced order-dependent accuracy, or specialized kernel constraints, our work reframes sequence packing as the classic bin packing challenge. Crucially, we demonstrate how these methods maintain mathematical equivalence with unpacked counterparts, allowing practitioners to adopt this efficient strategy within current pre-training and fine-tuning workflows.

This study challenges conventional wisdom by investigating how task diversity affects performance in meta-learning for low-data scenarios. Typically involving algorithms trained on multiple few-shot tasks using sampled support and query examples classified into few classes per task, the work demonstrates a modification where support sets are fixed, thereby limiting task variety. Surprisingly, we find evidence suggesting that this modification does not only mitigate potential negative effects but consistently enhances performance across a variety of meta-learning frameworks and datasets. The paper presents several analytical observations to explain this phenomenon and acts to (i) deepen the inquiry into support set construction within meta-learning and provide simple yet competitive generalizable baselines for low-data settings.

Geophysical and atmospheric flow simulations depend on parametrizations for subgrid-scale processes because their grid resolution is often too coarse. Although physical understanding and mathematical approximations have led to notable advancements in closure or parametrization models for these processes, they remain imperfect, frequently resulting in forecast inaccuracies. Recent developments show that deep learning excels at capturing intricate patterns from detailed time-space datasets, thereby creating superior parametrization models for achieving more accurate large-scale simulations. However, practical application remains difficult due to failures in adhering to physical laws and issues with training generalization over diverse scenarios. This study introduces a frame-invariant approach designed to enhance both the precision and generalization of machine-learned closure models by integrating physical symmetries directly into the architecture of the convolutional neural network. Using a two-dimensional turbulent decay case dominated by the enstrophy cascade for evaluation, we utilized specific specialized layers that guarantee adherence to desired constraints through structural design, eliminating the need for auxiliary regularization. Our results indicate that the resulting symmetric model: (1) calculates subgrid-source terms with high accuracy, (2) satisfies fundamental physics through translation, rotation, and Galilean invariance by design, and (3) remains numerically stable when applied to different Reynolds numbers and initialization variations in grid-coarse flows by leveraging invariance. Furthermore, as noted in our analysis, we have constructed a link between traditional physics-guided theory and data-centric paradigms—a strategy particularly useful in advancing physically sound, turbulence-closing data models.

Utilizing simple digital cameras for collision avoidance enables the secure inclusion of miniature unmanned aerial vehicles within dense, low-altitude spaces. This research proposes such a defense mechanism, which combines an individual monococular camera with a hybrid neural network and path controller. Specifically, the architecture integrates vision-based depth estimation, a high-level regulatory sub-network, an entity impact forecasting module, an emergency decision process. Experimenting the system on a simulated flying robot navigating an obstacle field within an restricted trajectory, demonstrates that it can significantly decrease accident frequency whilst preserving practical operational velocities.

Developing efficient techniques for uncertainty quantification in kinetic equations is a challenging task primarily driven by the models' high dimensionality, which often makes computation computationally unsustainable. Conversely, this "curse of dimensionality" has motivated extensive research into building simplified approximations that reduce computational expense while yielding viable solutions. Many researchers have already explored such approximations using moment-equation closures and simplified collision models. Given this background, it is logical to leverage these simpler models within a multi-fidelity framework for uncertainty quantification: here, the full kinetic equation acts as a high-fidelity model, while the simplified schemes function as low-fidelity surrogate proxies. This article surveys recent advances in multi-fidelity approaches for solving the uncertainty quantification problems inherent in kinetic equations by strategically combining high- and low-fidelity assessments, specifically addressing compressible and incompressible hydrodynamic limits. We concentrate on two primary methodologies: multi-fidelity control variate methods and bi-fidelity stochastic collocation methods. Our analysis evaluates diverse approaches considering both the surrogate structures and associated numerical techniques employed. Due to the critical impact of surrogate choice, the presentation follows a practical, application-centric methodology across the various techniques reviewed.

This work presents a comprehensive expansion of a rapid communication by the author (Phys. Rev. B, 27(2):04567, 2005), which focused on simulating water adsorption onto graphite. This current study details enhanced methodologies, physical parameters, and results to provide greater utility for the readership. Grand canonical Monte Carlo simulations coupled with multistage histogram reanalysis have been employed to determine water adsorption isotherms on a graphite substrate, leveraging SPC/E empirical water potentials, a specific 10-12 potential, and newer multipolar models. We introduce a new method for automating grayscale image colorizing that integrates a pre-trained U-Net model with Fusion Layer features. This strategy enables the system to derive colorizing capabilities directly from the established properties of the pre-trained network, while simultaneously using the Fusion layer to synthesize results by harmonizing localized data from small patches with global class-based priors across the entire image, thereby producing visually superior outcomes. Current object detection models typically rely on a shared source domain distribution between training and testing datasets. However, this assumption frequently fails during real-world deployment, where models are exposed to novel environments. To counter domain shifts resulting from these conditions, Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) is widely used. Existing UDA techniques usually follow an offline approach, adapting the model to the target domain initially and then freezing it. Yet, this strategy is inadequate for real-life settings where models must constantly adapt to evolving domain shifts. Consequently, a practical UDA framework capable of continuously handling new shifts deployed in real time is urgently needed. To achieve this, we introduce a novel, unified framework for improving target domain performance through continuous online learning. Specifically, this includes MemXformer—an attention-mechanism based transformer and memory system that leverages incoming domain shifts without explicit feedback while capturing target distribution prototypes. These patterns generate robust positive and negative pairs, which inform an advanced contrastive loss function tailored as highly discriminative for the target domain. Empirical validation on various benchmarks demonstrates that this method achieves state-of-the-art accuracy for both online and offline adaptive scenarios. To date, this is a unique investigation addressing object detection across consecutive online and traditional offline adaptation settings. Code is accessible on their respective Github repository.

Recent studies on interpretable machine learning in natural language processing predominantly apply feature scoring techniques to determine the critical input components behind predictions. However, prior research indicates that no single scoring strategy consistently outperforms others across diverse text classification tasks, and users often rely on ad-hoc decisions regarding rationale characteristics, such as length and continuity. Motivated by this, we introduce a robust, adaptable framework that automatically selects the optimal feature scoring approach, rationale length, and rationale type on a per-example basis for a specific data point. Drawing from the principles of input erasure—under the assumption that faithful rationales are characterized by the maximal difference between a model's full-text predictions and those after rationale removal—this method tailors explanations effectively. Experiments across four standard text classification datasets reveal that our approach generates explanations with superior faithfulness, comprehensiveness, and sufficiency relative to fixed strategies. Significantly, practitioners leveraging this method need to make zero ad-hoc selections regarding scoring functions or rationale properties.

While the Coupled Automated Search Heuristics (CASH) challenge has extensively covered the automated configuration of ML pipelines—with numerous tools and solvers readily available—these solvers currently lack direct support for incorporating black-box limitations such as fairness, robustness, or other custom domain-specific requirements. We demonstrate how our methodology from [Liu, et al., 2020], which adapts the ADMM optimization framework to decompose the CASH task into multiple smaller sub-problems, enables the effective inclusion of these challenging non-monotonic constraints.

A pivotal element of the ATLAS detector's Phase-II Upgrade involves substituting the existing Inner Detector with the all-silicon ATLAS Inner Tracker (ITk), comprising pixel and strip trackers. The ITk strip tracker sensors were designed to endure the enhanced radiation levels anticipated following the High Luminosity upgrade at CERN, where a surge in collision and track rates is expected. Operating within the ATLAS detector, these sensors are projected to experience sensitronic fluences of up to 1.6 x 10^15 n_eq/cm^2—accounting for a 1.5 safety factor—which will profoundly impact their performance. A key characteristic for such highly irradiated sensors is the uniformity and configuration of the electric field across their active regions. The presented results focus on diodes, manufactured with edge structures mimicking the full-scale ATLAS sensors, which were exposed to irradiation levels akin to those in the ITk strip tracker. The shape and extent of the electric field were then charted at various applied bias voltages using micro-focused X-ray imaging (beam dimensions: 2x3 µm^2). Furthermore, this research delineates how depletion zone evolution with irradiation allows for an evaluation of experimentally derived leakage currents against theoretical predictions, correlating measured performance with expected active areas.

Bayesian optimization successfully identifies the extremes of black-box functions. Our study proposes a new Bayesian optimization approach tailored for understanding user preferences within high-dimensional spaces. The core premise is that the objective function is inaccessible for direct evaluation; instead, we can query the minimizer of the projection and refer to this mechanism as an "optimizing preferential query." The query format facilitates natural human feedback that promotes interactivity. A user experiment confirms that such feedback, manifested as an optimal position and orientation of a molecule adsorbing a surface, corresponds effectively to such queries. Our framework is shown capable of discovering the global minimum of an infeasible-to-solve black box function that challenges state-of-the-art Bayesian methods that rely for optimization solely upon pairwise comparisons.

Stochastic parameterizations address uncertainties regarding unresolved sub-grid dynamics by sampling from the distribution of feasible forces. Although existing methods often use data-driven strategies to quantify this uncertainty, they frequently rely on heavy structural constraints that restrict their scalability. Conversely, machine learning frameworks—including neural networks—offer the ability to model diverse distributions effectively and establish robust mappings from numerous inputs to sub-grid forcings to date, recent investigations have been limited exclusively to deterministic parameterization. This research introduces a stochastic parameterization leveraging a generative adversarial network (GAN). We trained and evaluated the GAN-based system using data derived from the Lorenz '96 model, serving as a fundamental benchmark for assessing parameterization and data assimilation methods. The study examines various strategies for defining input noise and conducts experiments spanning both short-term (weather) and long-term (climate) scales. A number of these configurations outpreform a custom baseline across both temporal regimes, while also faithfully capturing the spatio-temporal dynamics and regimes of the Lorenz '96 system. Further findings suggest that models generating high-skill weather forecasts inherently produce superior climate simulations.

In the pharmaceutical sector, visual inspection for opaque vaccines with suspensions is currently a tedious manual process reliant on human operators; however, we demonstrate that deep learning offers a superior method for automation. To effectively differentiate true anomalies from particulates, surface reflections, and dust on vials, a dynamic view is essential. Leveraging 3D-ConvNeT, we trained a model to classify 20-frame video sequences for the presence of anomalies based on a hand-labeled, unoctmented dataset sourced from vials supplied by the HAL Allergy Group. Upon bench-marking with ten randomly initialized 3D-ConvNeT networks, we observed mean average ROC (AUROC) scores of 0.94 and 0.93 for anomalous and non-anomalous instances, respectively. Employing generative models for frame-to-video augmentation introduced several advancements: first, a saliency-map computation algorithm confirmed that 3D-ConvNeT accurately detects anomalies; second, a novel self-training technique utilizes these maps to assess consensus in network localization decisions. This self-training strategy facilitated dataset augmentation by adding 217,888 new samples, resulting in models significantly outperforming those trained solely on the original unoctmented data.

The Transit Timing Variation (TTV) method serves as a robust technique for determining exoplanet masses by analyzing transit photometric data. We evaluated the capabilities of the Ariel satellite's Fine Guidance Sensors (FGS 1/2) using simulated light curves from both high-contrast targets like the bright 55 Cnc system and low-luminosity stars such as K2-24. Utilizing a Markov Chain Monte-Carlo (MCMC) framework, we quantified the transit timing uncertainty at the nominal 1-second sampling rate, comparing these results against scenarios employing 30-second and 60-second cadences. Our analysis indicates that at full speed, Ariels achieves a transit precision of roughly 12$ s$ and 34$ s$ when measuring signals from the bright 55 Cnc star and the faint K2-24 object, respectively. Subsequent dynamical simulations incorporated these timing uncertainties to show an estimated 20–30$\%$ enhancement in the precision of mass measurements for systems resembling that of K2-24 through TTV analysis. Additionally, our simulation modeling demonstrates the conditions under which Ariels, using just ten transit observations within a one-transit duration, can identify timing signals caused by as-yet-undetected external bodies ranging between Earth and Neptune in mass.

This paper introduces a new offline approach optimizing dynamic treatment regimess using a Bayesain pessimism method. We suggest enhancing such a mechanism by combining it with Bayesian machine learning methods and Thempson sampling, specifically to automatically optimize the level of the strategy's pessimism. We developed a precise range, defined as a crucial upper and lower bound for an optimal Q-function value, which can be uniformly estimated from the given strategy's boundary and therefore obviates any need for manual customization of the hyperparameter selection. We also built a general-purpose Bayessian learning procedure that accommodates various modeling structures spanning simple linear bases to more sophisticated recurrent neural networks. Lastly, we constructed the calculation algorithm through the tool of vaitional inference for greater efficiency and scalability while maintaining the current theoretical underpinings as valid, and demonstrated empirically using both created models and actual data instances that it outperforms existing leading techniques.

Direct imaging and precise characterization of exoplanets via Extreme Adaptive Optics (ExAO) stands as a primary scientific objective for forthcoming Extremely Large Telescopes (ELTs), a challenge already hampered in ground-based systems by wavefront errors. These limitations stem from quasi-static disturbances and remaining atmospheric residuals, the latter producing brief faults that accumulate into haloes over extended exposures. To address these dual issues for ground observatories, our team developed, devised, and validated the "Self-Coherent Camera" strategy known in the laboratory as the "FAST" (Fast Atmospheric SCC Technique). Drawing from recent and current advancements—spanning both theoretical simulations and practical laboratory work—this study highlights FAST's capacity: while numerical models demonstrate that present 10-meter telescopes could identify reflected light from exoplanets and thermally radiating exo-Jupiters, it might also enable the direct imaging of habitable worlds on future ELTs. Additionally, our laboratory efforts focus on presenting the first detailed assessments of the proposed, already-manufactured masks required for this advanced coronagraphic technique.

This study introduces a controller designed to achieve stable grasping of objects with irregular, previously unknown shapes using dual robotic fingers equipped with tactile skins. Stability is maintained through the mechanical rotation of fingertips against surfaces combined with the application of a target gripping force, driving the system toward equilibrium. The approach is verified both via simulation and through experimentation on a fully-activated Shadow Modular Grasper fitted with bespoke BRL TacTip-derived optical sensors; however, the controller depends on estimating contact surface orientations via a deep convolutional neural regression applied to tactile imagery. Results indicate the system can achieve stable equilibrium across objects with varied geometries and softness levels while resisting disturbances and measurement inaccuracies. Furthermore, the methodology holds potential for application to robust in-hand manipulation using multiple digits.

Notably, by substituting $m=1$, we recover new inequalities dedicated to standard convex functions.

We examine a smooth $2n$-manifold $M$ equipped with a bi-Lagrangian structure denoted by $(\omega, \mathcal{F}_{1}, \mathcal{F}_{2})$. In this context, $\omega$ constitutes a symplectic 2-form, while $(\mathcal{F}_{1}, \mathcal{F}_{2})$ represents a pair of transversal Lagrangian foliations within the symplectic manifold $(M, \omega)$. A key geometric component associated with these structures is the Hess Connection; particularly, these links are instrumental in the taxonomy of affine bi-Lagrangian systems. Our study demonstrates that a bi-Lagrangian structure defined on $M$ admits a lift as an identical bi-Lagrangian structure onto its product trivial bundle, $M\times\mathbb{R}^n$. Furthermore, when an affine bi-Lagrangian structure undergoes this process, its lifted counterpart remains an affine bi-Lagrangian structure. Within this work, we introduce a dynamic acting on both the symplectomorphism group and the set of bi-Lagrangian configurations, defining an action where the symplectomorphisms modify these structures to be preserved by affine transformations. When projected alongside the lifted dynamics, this approach extends to the bundle $(M\times\mathbb{R}^{2n})\times\mathbb{R}^{4n}$, where in specific instances on certain manifolds, this iterative lifting converges to match the original dynamic properties. Finally, these findings remain valid even if $M\times\mathbb{R}^{2n}$ substitutes for either the tangent bundle ($TM$), cotangent bundle ($T^*M$), of suitable manifolds $M$, respectively.

We develop a model based on a non-isothermal reaction-diffusion equation by synthesizing non-equilibrium thermodynamics principles with the energetic variational approach. This framework produces a general system describing the evolutionary dynamics of chemical reactions under general mass kinetics at variable temperatures. Consequently, we derive a linearized version applicable near-equilibrium states and demonstrate that the system possesses global well-posedness in space-time given small initial conditions defined in a specific Besov space.

This paper initiates the analysis of quantum algorithms for guaranteeing escape from saddle points. Contrasting this with the leading classical algorithm by Jin et al.—a gradient-based method (first-order) requiring $\tilde{O}(\log^{6}(n)/\epsilon^{1.75})$ queries—our approach achieves a polynomial improvement concerning $\log n$ while maintaining identical complexity for the $1/\epsilon$ terms. Our primary technical advancement involves substituting classical perturbations within gradient descent techniques with simulations of quantum wave equations, which yields this reduction in quantum query complexity by factors of $ \log n $. Furthermore, we demonstrate how to leverage Jordan’s method for quantum gradient calculation to convert classical gradient oracles into quantum evaluation oracles with equal computational cost. Finally, we conduct numerical experiments that corroborate these theoretical results.

Social health and emotional well-being have become critical concerns in today's contemporary metropolis. Urban residence negatively impacts psychological health by introducing increased stressors, including factors such as crowded conditions, pollution, frequent violence, and diminished social connections. However, it must be acknowledged that only flourishing citizens are capable of forming a truly intelligent city. Accordingly, this article proposes a fuzzy logic approach to evaluate human wellness by monitoring routine daily activities and performance. To achieve this, the multifaceted variables influencing well-being are categorized into three key components: physical fitness, productivity, and social engagement. Applying these specific parameters generates a comprehensive coefficient reflecting an individual's total well-being.

In recent times, the proliferation of distributed data at the edge devices has made centralized data collection for machine learning challenging, often due to legal and regulatory constraints. As a solution, Federated Learning (FL) offers an effective paradigm for co-modeling machine learning without transferring private raw data. FL involves selecting available computing resources, yet optimizing schedules across the concurrent jobs of such learning remains a significant, unresolved challenge to maintain performance without compromising fairness.

Addressing this, the present study offers an innovative multi-job FL architecture designed to enable simultaneous processing of independent training tasks. We propose Entanglement-assisted concatenated quantum codes (EACQCs) by linking two separate quantum codes, offering several distinct advantages over standard concatenated quantum codes (CQCs). Consequently, due to these capabilities for both superior communication and robustness, we show that EACSQC are not merely competitive for quantum information transmission, but viable tools for fault-tolerant quantum computation as well.

Nucleus-mediated protein import and export involve key cell cycle regulators. These processes undergo cyclic modulation as part of the cell cycle, exemplified by the periodic disassembly and reformation of the nuclear envelope. Consequently, replicated DNA segregates between two daughter cells while nuclear-localized proteins disperse into the cytoplasm through diffusion. This study employs a mathematical import-diffusion framework to illustrate the mechanism by which nuclei toggling between mitosis and interphase redistribute regulators. Additionally, we explore how various model parameters influence the velocity and spatial origin of these waves. We investigated a solar flare designated as X1.6, generated by NOAA AR 12602 on October 22, 2014. Observations captured the entire event through RHESSI, IRIS, and Hinode/EIS, facilitating an analysis of chromospheric reactions driven by nonthermal electrons. The injection event lasted 352 seconds with a cumulative energy of $4.8\times10^{30}$ erg, triggering an explosive evaporation of chromospheres. Observations identified distinct shifts in both Doppler and nonthermal velocities at a reversal flow temperature range of 1.35–1.82 MK. The injection peak, occurring at 14:06 UT, coincided with maximum velocities, characterized by 200 km s$^{-1}$ blueshifts in the generally static Fe XXIV channel core. Just prior to this peak, the nonthermal electrons displayed a spectral index of approximately 6, marking the highest nonthermal velocity in both Fe XXI and Si IV. Conversely, Fe XIV, forming near the reversal zone velocity temperatures, showed low nonthermal velocities that correlated poorly with density or Doppler shifts. Nonthermal velocity in ions with similar thermal conditions increased and aligned with Doppler flow measurements, indicating surrounding unresolved flows around the reversal point. This work offers an exhaustive, time-resolved set of chromospheric diagnostics alongside an energy injection profile for a significant X-class flare, providing a valuable dataset for subsequent modeling efforts.

Medical vision-and-language pre-training (Med-VLP) has garnered significant attention for its capability to derive general vision-and-language representations from medical imaging and textual data. Current approaches predominantly consist of three components: unimodal encoders (visual and language), a multimodal fusion mechanism, and pretext tasks. These studies rarely consider medical expert domain knowledge or explicitly utilize it to improve Med-VLP. Although knowledge-enhanced VLP exists for general fields, they typically rely on readily available toolsets like object detectors and scene graph parsers, which are lacking in healthcare. This paper introduces a systematic framework to boost Med-VLP by leveraging structured medical knowledge from three angles. In a human's cognitive architecture, remembering and forgetting serve as two interconnected aspects. While contemporary artificial machine systems, inspired by biological cognition, strive for lifelong learning by optimizing memory retention while treating forgetting as an obstacle to minimize, recent scholarship reveals they have grasped only half the story. Scholars now advocate the view that the human mind is inherently predisposed to forget, framing non-retainial memory erasure as a deliberate, active driver for forming abstract, versatile, and nuanced representations. This study introduces a learning framework within artificial neural networks that harnesses an active forgetting mechanism termed the Active Forgetting Model (AFM). A "plug-and-play"Forgetting Layer (P&PF) is integrated into the neural architecture, incorporating inhibitory neuronal clusters managed through Internal Regulation (IRS)—leveraging lateral inhibition to auto-adjust inhibition levels—paired with External Regulation (ERS), which modulates the decay rates of excitatory neurons through inhibition. Empirical results indicate that the P&PF significantly boosts self-adaptability, generalization capabilities, robust long-term learning and memory retention, as well as tolerance against data and parameter noise. Offering compelling evidence for the vital role of forgetting in education and computation, this research furnishes a novel lens for analyzing latent neural processing mechanisms.

This paper examines the non-equilibrium evolution of a three-state kinetic opinion exchange model featuring switchability between extreme states contingent on a parameter $q$. Measurement Error Mitigation (MEM) refers to postprocessing techniques designed to address persistent readout inaccuracies in quantum computing (QC). Advances in technology have now enabled access to high-resolution data concerning human temporal behaviors. Numerous approaches have since emerged to extract valuable research and business insights by mining these dynamic behavioral patterns. Nevertheless, the predominant strategies focus primarily on action sequences while largely overlooking inter-temporal elements, specifically the intervals between actions, from a holistic stance. Although actions and their temporal gaps are mutually dependent, combining them poses significant challenges due to their distinct characteristics—actions represent events while time represents quantity. To address this, we introduce a unified framework that simultaneously analyzes user behaviors along with their inter-temporal metrics. This method embeds action sequences and corresponding time intervals to generate a low-dimensional representation encompassing both aspects, allowing for action characterization within its temporal context. Validated using three real-world datasets, the study shows that explicit modeling of both action patterns and temporal intervals facilitates successful interpretable analysis of user behavior.

We categorize approaches under this overarching challenge of efficient line-segment formation into three configurations: separating point datasets, managing those scenarios within polygonally constrained environments with obstacles, and handling polygonal shapes intersected by both sets and obstacles in the latter. Pediatric Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia (ALL) represents approximately 80 percent of cases in children. This paper introduces bound-preserving discontinuous Galerkin (DG) methods tailored for chemical reactive flows. Developing effective numerical schemes involves several challenges: first, fundamental physical constraints dictate that internal energy must be positive while mass fractions must stay within the range [0, 1]. Second, rapidly reacting systems often contain stiff sources; attempting to resolve these with standard strong-stability-preserving explicit Runge-Kutta time-stepping can severely restrict the admissible time step sizes. To address these physical requirements, we integrate the bound-preserving technique directly into our DG framework. For temporal evolution, we employ modified Runge-Kutta/multi-step Patankar methods, which treat convective fluxes explicitly and stiff source terms implicitly. This hybrid approach enables the resolution of stiff sources without excessive time step restrictions while rigorously enforcing variable positivity and maintaining unit sum for mass fractions. However, reconciling bound-preserving DG spatial operators with Patankar-based time stepping poses specific difficulties. Traditional DG positivity-preserving strategies rely on ensuring non-negativity at cell interfaces, whereas the Patankar method guarantees the positivity of point-values. To harmonize the associated degrees of freedom, we utilize $Q^k$ polynomials on rectangular meshes for two-dimensional simulations. Our strategy involves evaluating polynomial values at Gaussian quadrature points, applying slope limiters there to secure positivity before they can propagate as non-negated numerical updates by the time integrator. Furthermore, a distinct set of bound-preserving DG techniques operates at the element edges for convective fluxes, necessitating another application of a slope limiter to derive strictly non-negative numerical values required for these constraints.

We also suggest an experimental method to detect entanglement-type transitions by analyzing temporal fluctuations within the subsystem.

Graph Signal Processing (GSP) traditionally relies on a shift operator to construct a Fourier basis for signal representation, typically derived to reflect the graph's topology. Under our approach, a generalized convolution filter is interpreted as the expected value of random classical convolution operators, whereas bandlimitedness necessitates a broader interpretation than the standard fixed point of a band-pass filter. Furthermore, we provide a mechanism to translate operators between different spaces, enhancing applicability across diverse scenarios. Numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets confirm that GSP over a probability space outperforms models limited to a single shift operator.

The two main challenges in calculating thermal vibrational correlation functions are examined. The first issue stems from the failure of a single well-behaved mathematical expression to remain valid across both high-temperature conditions and the $T \to 0$ K limit. For instance, evaluating the propagator and partition function independently often results in a 0/0 indeterminate form near absolute zero; however, this problem is solved within the harmonic approximation when treating them jointly, which eliminates a problematic zero-point energy term derived from the propagator and yielding a deterministic function at low temperatures. The second challenge involves the inherent multivalued nature of the vibrational correlation function. Numerical evidence demonstrates that incorrect branch choices produce discontinuities in the computed function and lead to erroneous vibronic spectra. To rectify this, a phase-tracking methodology is suggested to maintain continuity in the real and imaginary components of the correlation function, thereby achieving accurate spectral recovery. These claims are substantiated through simulations of the UV-vis absorption spectra for benzene at 298 K and pentacene at 4 K; in both cases, the calculated results align well with experimental data.

Smart grids utilize data from smart meters to drive critical operational choices but face significant risks from False Data Injection (FDI) attacks, where adversaries alter meter readings to interfere with grid functioning. Current research often adopts a simplified model assuming a single operator accesses all data with only partial meter compromise. To secure such a system, operators must collaborate by sharing data. The paramount challenge is creating motivation for this data sharing. We tackle this by proposing an incentive mechanism that recompenses operators for submitting data yet penalizes missingness or anomalous values. We establish formal conditions proving that this mechanism resists operators motivated by profit to withhold or manipulate measurements. Furthermore, we deploy a blockchain-based solution to facilitate data sharing, incorporating optimizations to evade blockchain-specific performance deficits. Substantial experimental analysis confirms our implementation delivers practical real-world efficiency.

Anomaly detection remains a vibrant research area where identifying low-probability events is particularly difficult due to the data's high dimension and the scarcity of a priori information regarding anomalies. Although many existing methods exist, most fail to handle large-scale datasets efficiently and rely on the setting of sensitive hyperparameters. We introduce an unsupervised technique for anomaly and change detection in remote sensing images, utilizing a multivariate Gaussianization method capable of estimating multivariate densities precisely—a historically challenging task. Experiments on various distant imaging configurations highlight its efficiency, proving that it surpasses both linear and nonlinear counterparts in detection capability. Establishing significant distances between samples within a dataset represents a core challenge in machine learning. Optimal Transport (OT) elevates distances based on specific features (the "ground metric") into geometrically meaningful metrics applicable to sample distributions. Nevertheless, selecting the appropriate ground metric often involves substantial difficulty; while supervised methods requiring labeled data exist for this task, unsupervised alternatives generally rely on arbitrary manual specifications. Consequently, learning ground metrics without supervision is critical for facilitating label-free OT applications. We present a novel approach that concurrently computes an OT distance between samples in one dimension and features in another, marking a first in this canonical formulation. The resulting distance matrices arise naturally as the positive singular vectors of the linear function defined by the progression from ground metrics to OT distances and the derived conditions ensure these vectors exist and remain unique when normalized by the input metric structure. We develop viable algorithms for efficiently approximating these distances even in very high-dimensional spaces using stochastic analysis and entropic regularization techniques. The methods have been validated and visualized through analysis of a real-case single-cell RNA-sequencing dataset.
