Estimating the Post-Click Conversion Rate (CQR) (CVR) represents a foundational research challenge for developing effective recommender systems, notably hindered by sample selection bias and sparse data. Existing entire space multi-task models, which mitigate data sparsity by exploiting user behavioral sequences such as "exposure → click → conversion," fail to provide guaranteed CVR unbiasedness. This research identifies and details inherent estimation bias (IEB) (1) (undermining the independence of CVV estimators and potentially leading to over-estimation of ground truth metrics); and potential propagation inconsistency (PIPI); and PIP (PIPI - Propagation Inconsistency), where the causal linkage from click through to conversions may be disregarded. Contemporary life is filled with myriad paying and free services, ranging from video subscription streams to car-sharing and digital ticket purchases. Online vendors typically distribute tokens tied directly to user identities after registration, necessitating repeated authentication with the same credentials. Similarly, physical services, such as purchasing an entry pass to a concert, rely on a ticket that validates a customer's entitlement to access. Common drawbacks across both digital and in-person models include system centralization and inadequate protection of user privacy. Companies offering these amenities act as Service Providers or Trusted Third Parties, managing both service delivery and the confidential data of their clients. FORT is presented and developed in this study as a centralized-blockchain-free solution: it empowers users to authenticate their right to utilize select services, regardless of format, while safeguarding private sensitive data. Through blockchain infrastructure, we establish the mechanism for achieving full distribution; user rights are uniquely minted via Non-Fungible Tokens (NFTs). Possession and the verification of these tokens rely exclusively on Zero-Knowledge Proofs—cryptogenic primitives ensuring total privacy. Moreover, we offer performance benchmarks demonstrating the system's suitability for mobile devices equipped with minimal computing capacity—such as smartphones and smartwear—which represent typical use cases in such applications.

We introduce a protocol for creating multipartite entanglement via the coherent control of trapped atoms confined within an optical cavity. By utilizing cavity-mediated interactions alongside two control beams, we demonstrate the adiabatic production of entanglement, yielding high-quality resources optimized for our proposed measurement strategy. We outline the experimental realization of our approach, benchmarking the output states against classical systems and ideal maximally-entangled Dicke configurations. Results reveal distinct metric superiority for our generated states; while achieving metrological gain consistently, our protocol surpasses even perfect Dicke states when sensing magnetic field gradients. Given the protocol's inherent scalability, it presents a robust framework for advanced quantum state engineering.

Research on few-shot object detection frequently integrates meta-learning into region-based frameworks, yet this approach remains hindered by challenges such as the generation of unreliable region proposals for new categories and insufficient attention to inter-class relationships. Operating solely at the image level, Meta-DETR bypasses the issue of inaccurate proposal generation plaffing other frameworks, while simultaneously attending to multiple reference classes via a single feed-forward operation. Consequently, it actively captures relationships between different classes to effectively manage misclassifications among similar entities and robustly generalize knowledge to unknown categories. Evaluation on standard metrics reveals that Meta-DETR substantially surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques. This work examines the photonic band structure physics arising from overlapping two uni-dimensional (1D) photonic crystal slabs with mismatched lattice constants. Our system's spectrum results from a competition between intra-layer and inter-layer interaction mechanisms, adjustable by varying the spacing between the two slabs. We establish an effective Hamiltonian that encapsulates the system's fundamental principles and replicates numerical electromagnetic simulations with high fidelity. Notably, "magic distances"—specific separations that generate photonic flatbands across the entirety of the photonic moir\'{e} superlattice Brillouin zone—are discovered. Furthermore, we show that these flatband modes remain highly confined within a single moir\'{e} period interval and introduce a single-band tight-binding description for the resulting moir\'{e} minibands; in this framework, the tunneling velocity can be readily modified through changes in inter-layer interaction strength. Our findings demonstrate that the band structure engineering of bilayer photonic moir\'{e} lattices aligns precisely with the manipulation of electronic or excitonic moir\'{e} structures. These insights may facilitate investigations into many-body physics at moir\'{e} photonic flatband systems and enable the development of advanced optoelectronic applications.

Recently, Distributed Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL) has generated significant interest, largely driven by advancements in Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). To address these issues, we propose Multi-Agent Adaptive Kalman Temporal Difference (MAK-TD) and its Successor Representation-based extension (MAK-SR). The core of this framework harnesses the distinct capabilities of Kalman Filtering, notably its ability to model uncertainty and perform second-order online learning. Designed for continuous high-dimensional action spaces inherent to multiplayer environments, the MAK-TD/SR approach utilizes Kalman Temporal Difference (KTD) principles to mitigate parameter uncertainty. Additionally, Successor Representation learning is reformulated as a filtering problem using Radial Basis Function (RFB) estimators to map continuous states to feature vectors, while Multiple Model Adaptive Estimation (MMAE) facilitates spatial reward learning in the face of unknown observation noise and state mappings. The efficacy of MAK-TD and MAK-SR validates through extensive experiments conducted on OpenAI Gym MARL benchmarks.

We introduce MC-CIM, a novel compute-in-memory framework that enables efficient, Bayesian edge intelligence for deep neural networks. To mitigate this, Bayesian inference has emerged as a method that extracts not only predictions but also their confidence levels for risk-aware decision-making; however, full Bayesian approaches remain too costly for real-time edge deployments. To bridge this gap, we explore Monte Carlo Dropout (MC-Dropout), which offers high robustness with significantly lower computational demands but currently requires format optimization to address its processing bottlenecks. Our work presents an innovative MC-CIM module capable of performing in-memory weight-input scalar products and probabilistic dropout operations. We further propose a computational reuse formulation of MC-Dropout, allowing each iteration to leverage the computations of its predecessor. Additionally, we apply combinatorial optimization to arrange input sampling sequences efficiently and reduce total workload. We evaluate the proposed MC-CIM on MNIST character recognition and drone visual odometry using a configuration with 086x43 SRAM units operating on 086V at standard temperature and ambient air (16nm LSTP). The resulting inference consumes approximately 7 degrees energy per frame. Experimental results show that despite constraints, MC-CIM successfully maintains robust performance with minimal overhead. Notably, restricting prey movement broadly fosters inhomogeneous steady states across extensive parameter landscapes, significantly boosting persistence at all spatial resolutions, including the local level. We further demonstrate that these qualitative patterns hold true for broad classes of complex networks comprising many patches. Additionally, we derived various stability conditions for inhomogeneous steady states, a performance level that is firmly rooted in prior simulation results. Consequently, our insights regarding limited dispersal offer a foundation for developing targeted conservation strategies.

This paper addresses motion planning under the uncertainty that recommended routes from satellite navigational systems (GPS or "Satnavs") often do not follow the shortest paths. Although the system indicates an arc leading toward the destination $H$ (home) with high confidence $p$ at every decision node $Q$ of network $\mathfr�$, adhering strictly to this suggestion can paradoxically result in an infinite loop. To minimize the *expected* time required to reach $H$, what optimal probability $q$—a function of network topology $q(Q,p)$—should the system assign this route suggestions to, otherwise selecting a random alternative? We label this scenario the Faulty GPS or "Satnav" Problem. We explore extensions allowing $q$ to fluctuate based on local connectivity (node degree), and investigate competitive scenarios where search parties race to locate $H$ (akin to a "treasure hunt"). While the primary analogy involves vehicles navigating real-time GPS failures, this framework applies broadly to any autonomous agent, such as an unmanned air vehicle (UAV), operating under faulty positional data; the challenge originates not merely from commuter frustration but stems from Fonio et al. (2017) regarding insect navigation, where pheromone trails guide foragers back to the colony regardless of path length. Crucially, whether a robot car, ant, driver, or algorithm cannot deduce the probabilistic generation rules of suggested path segments, categorizing these challenges within operational research concerning the optimal degree of trust placed in probabilistic suggestions made by artificial systems.

Motivation for decentralized learning has driven extensive research recently due to the framework common to federated learning. Although most prior studies focus on an offline context with static objective functions, these scenarios often become impractical when faced with the vast and evolving data streams in many application domains. In this study, we introduce \emph{decentralized online} methods tailored for convex and continuous DR-submodular optimization---function classes prevalent in numerous machine learning tasks. Proposed algorithms deliver performance benchmarks comparable to the centralized offline approach while ensuring that, on average, each agent computes gradients for just one time step. Additionally, we broaden these strategies to the bandit scenario. Ultimately, we demonstrate the strong competitive efficiency of our proposed methods across real-world experiments.

This study addresses non-rigid shape matching within the functional map framework, critically evaluating the widely adopted strategy of regularizing functional maps through the penalty function designed to ensure their commutation with the Laplace-Beltrami operators of both the source and target shapes. We demonstrate that this traditional method possesses intrinsic theoretical flaws, occasionally becoming undefined even when applied to trivial, smooth maps. In response, we introduce an alternative, robustly theorized methodology for regularisation that leverages the concept of the Laplacian's resolvent. Beyond this core proposal, our work defines a controllable one-parameter family of regulators, allowing precise tuning based on anticipated degrees of isometry in given shape pairs. Through extensive experimentation across various correspondence scenarios, our findings indicate that the proposed regularization not only elevates the precision of the estimated functional map but also results in markedly superior point-to-point correspondences, beneficial before as well as after standard post-refinement processes.

Population protocols are a fairly recent distributed computing paradigm where anonymous agents operating under severe constraints communicate pairwise to evaluate predicates. We examine a probabilistic variant of this framework, which accepts a minimal risk of incorrect outputs. Our thesis centers on probabilistic confidential leader election, an enhanced version of the standard leader selection task requiring the elected agent to eventually confirm its status as a singleton leader. This uniqueness verification is valuable because it helps distinguish when the protocol has fully converged; while this behavior has proved achievable through various extensions of the original model, it presents unique challenges here. Our analysis demonstrates that any probabilistic protocol capable of reaching a stable balance with all states represented (where a portion of agents resides in every reachable state from an initial homogeneous state) necessarily demands a number of interactions linear relative to population size. Consequently, achieving confident leader generation remains infeasible within the probabilistic model.

Real-time, photo-realistic rendering is essential for realizing some of the most thrilling metaverse capabilities, particularly live interactions within virtual environments. However, current active and passive 3D reconstruction methods for such rendering often demand substantial manual cleanup of point clouds and meshes. To address this gap, we introduce Neural Volumetric Video (NeuVV), a neural volumetric rendering method that enables real-time, spatial-temporal, photo-realistic, versatile, and interactive videostatistical content processing.

NeuVV centers on an efficient encoding of a dynamic Neural Radiance Field into render-ready and editable primitives through a dual factorization approach. One scheme employs Hyper-Spherical Harmonics (HH) capture for streamlining the depiction of spatial and temporal color transitions, while a learnable basis captures abrupt motion-induced alterations to color and density. By integrating this factorization into a Volumetric Octree (V-Occtree) architecture, akin to Plein-Octrees, the method substantially accelerates training periods while lowering memory consumption.

Consequently, real-time NervvV rendering paves the way for advanced content editing instruments that treat each VOCtreen as distinct primitives; these supports utilize volume-based ordering and alpha compositing to facilitate spatio-temporal assembly for video reuse. Examples include placing varying representations of a single performance across diverse coordinates with distinct timing, dynamically altering fabric textures/clothes hues, rendering spotlight casts and shadows, synthesizing distance lighting effects—and all these modifications occur interactively. Furthermore, we present a novel mixed raster-voxeleration-based NVV (hyblized) rendering architecture, empowering consumer-grade head-mounted displays, thereby enabling volumetric video editing and consumption within an inherently 23-space VR context for the first time.

Code summarization focuses on automatically producing natural language descriptions for specific code fragments, a capability that significantly aids developers in grasping code functionality and supporting maintenance tasks. Current approaches divide into two main categories: extraction-based techniques, which select crucial statements and keywords via retrieval processes to ensure factual accuracy, but often suffer from unnatural naming conventions and phrasing; and ablation-based techniques, which leverage encoder-decoder models similar to those in neural machine translation to generate fluent text, though these may overlook key factual specifics. To balance human-readable fluency with essential detail preservation, we introduce an innovative extraction-summation hybrid framework. Within this model, the extraction component identifies code statements rich in factual relevance from the provided snippet, while the abstraction module concurrently processes the entire code section and these selected statements to synthesize a concise, naturally flowing summary. Evaluating this approach, dubbed EACS, through extensive testing across datasets covering six distinct programming languages, the findings reveal a significant performance surpassment over state-of-the-art solutions across all standard evaluation metrics: ROUGH-L.

We propose a machine-learning algorithm to generate measurement matrices for compressive sensing recovery tasks, with a specific emphasis on constant modulus (CM) constraints that correspond to analog phase shifter networks in hybrid précoding systems. By viewing a restricted isometry property (RIP) under CM constraints as the projection of points onto a lower-dimensional hypersphere, we hypothesize that achieving a uniform point distribution within this range would enhance resistance to noise. This principle is formalized as an optimization problem that incorporates maximum mean discrepancy (MWD) metrics into its objective function; encouraged by the recent success of such metrics in neural network applications, we apply learning-based techniques to solve it. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the resulting algorithm out performs random measurement matrices typically utilized in compressive sensing. Moreover, we integrate a traditional method compatible with both the CM constraints and random matrix benchmarks, finding it particularly effective when used to initialize the proposed learning-based approach. Finally, our framework outlines how to incorporate additional structural constraints, such as the Toeplitz structure.

Automated Speech Recognition (ASR) poses significant difficulties, particularly when trained with scarce audio data, which is a critical hurdle for low-resource languages. To address this training data deficit, we introduce a method combining Automated Curriculum Learning with an adversarial bandit algorithm derived from Reinforcement Learning. This framework is designed to reorder mini-batches according to their learning difficulty and evaluate its impact as measured against both baseline transfer-learning benchmarks and fixed curriculum strategies. Tested on a genuinely low-resource language, our results demonstrate that the bandit-based framework achieves significant improvements over the transfer-learning baseline models.

This manuscript demonstrates that noise-activated escape is possible even within confined Hamiltonian systems. Noise-induced energy fluctuations cause isopotential curves to open, enabling particles to escape in a finite timeframe. Consequently, the bounded dynamics shifts into a chaotic scattering problem. We examine this escape dynamics using average escape times, probability basins, and escape time distributions. Our results show that the scattering features in noisy closed Hamiltonian systems differ significantly from those in noisy open counterparts. Notably, whereas noise-enhanced trapping is prevalent across Hamiltonian systems, it is not central to the escape process here. A key finding reveals that increasing the noise induces a transition in the average escape time, demarcating two distinct regimes defined by different algebraic scaling laws. We present robust numerical evidence indicating that the full destruction of KAM island stickiness underpins the change in these scaling laws. Such research opens doors to modeling chaotic scattering through noisy closed Hamiltonian systems and suggests applicability in physics domains including celestial and astrophysical mechanics.

We scrutinized how size constraints influence thermoelectric phenomena in layered strongly correlated cobaltate thin films. While thermopower remains thickness-independent down to 6 nm at room temperature—an anomalous trend contradicts the Fuchs-Sondheimer model applicable to typical metals and semiconductors—we attribute this behavior to intense electron correlations. As anticipated, resistivity exhibits systematic variations with reduced thickness, becoming significantly altered below roughly 30 nm, even though temperature-dependent thermopower profiles stay comparable across different layers. These studies underscore the distinctive thermoelectric responses between correlated and uncorrelated systems under limited size conditions. By applying the atomic limit Hubbard model at its high-temperature boundary, we elucidate our observations. Ultimately, this research offers novel perspectives on disentangling electrical conductivity from thermopower within strongly correlated regimes.

Monitoring the city road infrastructure plays a vital role in enhancing the efficiency of transportation networks and overall urban functioning. Present monitoring methods rely heavily on inductive loop sensors, roadside cameras, and crowdsourced data (e.g., Google Maps); however, these approaches are plagued by challenges such as high expenses, sparse geographic coverage, and questionable reliability stemming from insufficient driver participation. This research explores an innovative drive-by sensing method that utilizes extensive fleets of ridesourcing vehicles to track and deduce urban road conditions as they traverse various streets. We evaluate fleet sensing capability through three metrics: explicit coverage via the count of visited road segments, redundancy achieved through multiple repeated visits, and potential inferred insights based on existing data and network topology. We introduce an optimal re-routing framework designed to simultaneously maximize sensing scope and reliability, utilizing a heuristic algorithm to efficiently manage the routes of idle vehicles for sequential deployment. Comprehensive experiments utilizing real-world telemetry from over 20,000 ridesourcing cars in New York City validate the model's efficacy and robustness through detailed sensitivity analysis. Our approach successfully monitors at least 75.5% of road segments, resulting in 97.2% imputation of network coverage—crucially, it boosts sensing reliability significantly, offering over a 31% performance lift compared to baseline strategies.

Forecasts for both short-term (one-day) and medium-term (ten-day) horizons were generated across various financial indices. Conventional robust recommendation approaches typically classify atypical user-item interactions as noise, employing filtering techniques to minimize their effects. However, this prevalent strategy often grapples with significant limitations. Initially, real-world scenarios indicate that unusual interactions frequently reflect a user's transient interest distinct from their baseline preferences; consequently, indiscriminately suppressing these interactions as noise can harm recommendation personalization. Secondly, identifying temporary interest proves challenging due to the scarcity of explicit supervisory signals that delineate typical from atypical engagements. To mitigate these challenges, we introduce Temporary Interest Aware Recommendation (TIARec), a framework designed to separate atypical from standard interactions without reliance on supervision, while effectively capturing both fleeting and stable user interests. Central to our solution is a reinforcement learning architecture comprising a primary recommendation agent and a secondary classifier agent engaged in joint training optimized for the cumulative returns of recommendations generated by the recommendation agent. Throughout their collaborative learning process, the classifier agent assesses interactions proposed by the recommendation agent to identify anomalies and delineate moments of specific, time-limited user preference; insights derived from handling atypical interactions regarding temporary interest are shared between models, enabling the recommendation agent to function independently with the ability to equilibrate a user's transient and inherent preferences. Finally, extensive evaluations performed across multiple real-world datasets affirm the efficacy of TIARec.

The concept of eigenstate thermalization in quantum many-body contexts suggests that high-energy states resemble random vectors. Discovering instances where certain states remain non-thermal remains an unresolved challenge. This study demonstrates that linked quantum models with a nullspace—a zero-energy, highly degenerate subspace equivalent to infinite temperature—offer a gateway to non-thermal states. We provide analytical proof for a specific class of local Hamiltonians where a single product-state zero mode exists. Extending to broader scenarios, we employ a subset disentangling method to construct an orthogonal basis of these zero modes exhibiting gradually increasing entanglement entropy. Our findings support an area-law scaling pattern for the least entangled zero mode across a wide parameter space, fueling the proposition that all such Hamiltonians possess zero modes adhering to area laws and consequently violating the strong eigenstate thermalization hypothesis. Additionally, zero modes have been detected within restricted frameworks, with proposed arrangements for their potential experimental verification.

Additive and generalized additive models serve as efficient semiparametric approaches for analyzing multidimensional data. This article introduces a novel smoothing backfitting method applied to generalized additive models using local polynomial smoothers. The core approach relies on a second-order expansion to approximate nonlinear integral equations aimed at maximizing local quasilikelihood. By storing coefficients as sufficient statistics, the method enables online updates through a dynamic candidate bandwidth strategy. This updating process relies exclusively on stored sufficient statistics and new incoming data batches. Additionally, the authors derive the asymptotic normality and lower bounds for the relative efficiency of these online estimates, offering insights into the trade-offs between estimation precision and computational costs dictated by segment length. Validated by simulations and real-data applications, the findings support the efficacy of this framework.

In recent years, research in skeleton-based action recognition has gained significant traction. However, many mainstream approaches face a fundamental constraint: sparsely represented skeleton data alone cannot fully encapsulate human kinetics. This limitation renders existing methods unreliable when tasked with categorizing actions that possess only minimal distinctive variations. To address this, we introduce a novel architecture termed JOLO-GCN, a dual-stream graph convolutional network that integrative a human pose skeleton with compact joint-focused visual cues generated using Joint-aligned optical and Flow (VAP)s patches. By capturing fine-grained movements surrounding individual joints, our hybrid approach delivers significant accuracy gains over pure skeleton-based baselines while maintaining computational and memory efficiencies. Comprehensive evaluations on NTU RGB+D, NTU RGB+D 120, and the Kinetics-Skeleton datasets corroborate these performance improvements compared to current state-of-the-art techniques.
